title: Benn does not deserve world title shot - Garcia
description: Ryan Garcia says Conor Benn is nothing more than an "average fighter" and does not deserve a shot at his WBC welterweight title.
fullText:
Ryan Garcia says Conor Benn is nothing more than an "average fighter" and that the Briton does not deserve a shot at his WBC welterweight title.

Garcia, 28, makes the first defence of his belt against Benn at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Saturday.

The American has consistently dismissed Benn's ability during the build-up and, after skipping Tuesday's face-off, has been accused overlooking the 29-year-old.

But Garcia says he is not taking anything lightly as he aims for a 26th win in 29 bouts as a professional.

Asked whether Benn, who has not fought at welterweight since April 2022, deserves the opportunity to challenge for a world title, Garcia said: "Not at all."

He told BBC Sport: "He's an average fighter, he's athletic and it's his last name. It's not a shot at him; it's just the bitter truth.

"I'm preparing like he's the best fighter in the world. It's all about preparation and how sharp you are.

"People could say you're overlooking him. No, I'm calling it how I see it.

"Do you want me to say he's as good as Floyd Mayweather? He's not.

"He's alright. He comes forward and throws looping overhands. He's aggressive and will make him a rugged fight, but it's not something I haven't seen before."

Garcia and Benn have documented their fight camps on social media, but have presented their preparations in different ways.

Benn has posted videos of his training regime, while Garcia has been collaborating with influencers and making appearances in the WWE.

"He's not my cup of tea. I wouldn't want to hang out with him too much," Garcia said.

"He's a bit of a hypocrite and contradicts himself a lot. I am who I am - goofy and outgoing, making jokes and having fun.

"He is trying to say he's humble, but he's out here any chance in a Rolls Royce. He loves the lights.

"He thinks I'm like that, but I'm focused on my craft 100%."

title: Why is there an NFL game in Australia?
description: The NFL has so far played regular-season games in seven international countries but this week's trip to Australia represents a new frontier for the USA's biggest sports league.
fullText:
The NFL has so far played regular-season games in seven international countries but this week's trip to Australia represents a new frontier.

It is the NFL's first game in the Asia-Pacific region, with the USA's biggest sports league making its longest-ever road trip for the first of a record nine international games in 2026.

It will take place about 10,000 miles from the NFL's New York headquarters, in front of about 100,000 fans at the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground.

That means the Los Angeles Rams will 'host' the San Francisco 49ers on a more open oval field on Friday (01:35 BST).

But when NFL commissioner Roger Goodell visited the MCG for the first time in April, he said the historic arena "speaks to you", and it says "this is the right place to be".

American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?

Live NFL games have been broadcast in Australia since 1995 and a pre-season exhibition game was held in Sydney in 1999.

Local interest has soared since 2022, though, when the NFL made the global growth of American football a strategic priority.

The league pivoted away from a potential overseas franchise to playing more games internationally. It has invested in new markets before deciding whether to take a game there, holding year-round events to build the fanbase.

Australian players Jordan Mailata (Philadelphia) and Michael Dickson (Seattle) have also captured the imagination down under, playing for the past two Super Bowl winners.

According to the league, the number of fans in Australia has nearly doubled since 2022 to 8.8 million - almost one in three of the country's entire population.

That includes those flooding to one of the world's fastest-growing sports, flag football - the non-contact version of American football.

The NFL played a big part in flag being approved for its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028 and has expanded the sport from 10 schools in Australia to more than 500.

Now it aims to help flag football secure a spot at Brisbane 2032, with NFL executive Peter O'Reilly acknowledging that is a key reason for playing in Australia.

Being a sports-mad country, Australia was always on the NFL's radar, and after testing long-distance logistics with trips to Brazil in 2024 and 2025, the league felt ready to head down under.

Sydney and Perth were in the running but Melbourne is regarded as the nation's sports capital and the MCG is the biggest stadium in the southern hemisphere.

A deal was announced in February 2025, during Super Bowl week, and while some fans expressed anger at ticket prices when they went on sale in April 2026, they sold out in minutes.

The state of Victoria is reportedly paying up to A$15m, external (£8m) for the right to host the game but expects one of the state's biggest returns. Dublin enjoyed a tenfold return on its investment to stage its first NFL game last September.

Almost 50% of the MCG tickets were bought by fans outside Victoria or overseas, so about 50,000 fans will visit Melbourne this week.

'The G' is also right next to Melbourne Park, home of tennis' Australian Open, an ideal venue for a three-day fan festival, which began with a watch party for last night's season opener.

The NFL picked this year's Super Bowl week to announce that the 49ers will be the Rams' opponents in Melbourne, which created a buzz in Australia and California.

Not only are the Rams and 49ers regular Super Bowl contenders but they are also divisional rivals in the ultra-competitive NFC West. In addition, there is heaps of hype around the Rams.

With this season's Super Bowl being held in LA, they have gone all-in to reach the big game. First they traded for defensive stars Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie, which cemented them as championship favourites.

Then three-time defensive player of the year Aaron Donald returned from retirement and although the 35-year-old has not travelled to Australia, Garrett and McDuffie will both make their Rams debut at the MCG.

Fred Warner, Nick Bosa and George Kittle are set to return from injury for the 49ers, with Mike Evans making his debut.

The game will be broadcast live on Netflix, reaching more than 200 countries, while the Jonas Brothers will perform a half-time show.

Who will reach Super Bowl? - NFL predictions for 2026 season

California is 17 hours behind Melbourne and the flight takes about 16 hours. The previous longest for a regular-season game was about 12 hours to Sao Paulo, Brazil.

Yet the two teams have taken a completely different approach. The 49ers arrived in Melbourne last Friday while the Rams arrived the day before the game - just as they did for last year's comfortable win at Wembley over the Jacksonville Jaguars.

The huge time difference means that the game kicks off at 10:35 on Friday in Melbourne - which is Thursday evening in the United States: 17:35 on the west coast, 20:35 on the east.

While a morning start (local time) is virtually unheard of in the NFL, it's perfectly normal for fans used to watching cricket at the MCG.

The long flights and early start have thrown each teams' regular routine out of kilter. San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan admitted he was struggling to remember what day it was.

But having the game in week one gives each team the best chance to cope with the travel demands, rather than playing it later in the season.

Kelce's last dance? Five things to look out for in new NFL season

The NFL has committed to playing one more game in Melbourne in the next three years, with the possibility of another.

What sets Australia apart from other countries hosting international games is that ball-carrying sports are the most popular down under.

All seven Australians in the NFL converted from rugby, basketball or Australian rules football, and Australia has a huge pool of similar athletes with transferable skills.

The NFL has pledged to provide flag football kits to every school in Australia and opened an academy on the Gold Coast as it aims to tap into that talent, which could produce an international pipeline of players targeting the Olympics and the NFL.

title: Instagram boss says users will be ‘overwhelmed’ with brand content in algorithm-free world
description: Adam Mosseri says platform’s algorithm ‘feels like a black box’ but company trying to give users more control after Labor announces opt-out...
fullText:
Adam Mosseri says platform’s algorithm ‘feels like a black box’ but company trying to give users more control after Labor announces opt-out plan

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Instagram’s chief executive has said users will have a worse experience in an algorithm-free world, seeing more brand-related content, and spend less time on the app.

The comments come as the Australian government plans to give users the option to opt out of algorithms, with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announcing plans on Tuesday to require social media platforms to prompt users to choose between a feed of algorithm-recommended content or a reverse chronological feed of the pages users follow. Labor also plans to introduce a range of measures designed to address online harm on the sites.

In a briefing with journalists on Thursday to launch the company’s Algo Confessions series in Australia, Instagram’s chief executive, Adam Mosseri, did not comment directly on the Albanese government proposal but said Instagram had a range of algorithms in operation. Those include ranking which friends’ stories you see more often, or which users come up first in message suggestions based on interactions, as well as the algorithm that determines the content people see in their feeds.

The launch of the series in Australia is the first outside the US. It features celebrities and influencers detailing how Instagram determines what content ends up in a user’s feed, and how the user can have some control over that by adding or removing tags in their settings.

Mosseri said just a “very vocal minority” wants social media to go back to reverse chronological feeds, which he said would just incentivise people to post more.

“What ends up happening is the best way to get more reach is just to post more often and those who can afford to post the most often do and then therefore get the most reach,” he said.

“And it turns out your friends post a lot less than creators, who post a lot less than brands and companies.”

He said people would be “overwhelmed” with content from brands, and creators and friends would be drowned out.

“What happens is people become a bit less interested in the experience and they use it a lot less, which then means that there’s less reach to go around and people start to get more and more mad about the fact that their reach is going down because the overall pie gets smaller.”

He said engagement and user satisfaction goes down.

“It’s this interesting tension between what an individual might want and what happens when you actually explode that to the entire community,” he said.

“That’s not to say that ranking is perfect, it’s not, we make mistakes – one of the things that frustrates me about ranking is that we end up over-optimising for things that we can measure and undervaluing things that are more difficult to measure.”

Mosseri said Instagram’s ranking algorithm “feels like a black box” but was something Instagram was trying to give users more control over by opting out of certain topics in their recommendations.

He said in the future, Meta’s AI models could eventually allow users to talk to the app to understand why they are seeing certain types of content.

Mosseri said he did not believe the app to be the clinical definition of “addictive”.

“I don’t believe Instagram is addictive – I know that is controversial to say – I do think we often in English anyway conflate the way we colloquially use the word addicted … like ‘I’m addicted to this show and I’m binge watching it, which is not good for me’.”

He said clinically defined addictions have withdrawal symptoms, while social media does not have that effect, and “those things are different”.

Mosseri has made this claim before. Research has found some users can have an impulse to use a platform without being fully aware of it, and evidence shows frequent engagement with algorithms “alters dopamine pathways” that fosters dependency that is “analogous to substance addiction”.

In the landmark US court case centred on the addictive nature of Meta’s products, the company’s lawyer last month conceded to the court that it was “no dispute” people can struggle with social media, but the company has tools to address that. Meta later settled the case for US$18bn while denying any wrongdoing.

title: Aryna Sabalenka’s Reaction to Losing World No. 1 Ranking Goes Viral
description: ESPN captured Aryna Sabalenka’s candid reaction as Elena Rybakina ended her 99-week reign atop the WTA rankings. The post Aryna Sabalenka’s Reaction to Losing World No. 1 Ranking Goes Viral appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
Aryna Sabalenka heard the roar before she saw what had happened.

The top-ranked player in women's tennis was practicing on Court P1 beside Arthur Ashe Stadium when the crowd erupted Wednesday afternoon. Sabalenka walked toward the televisions at the U.S. Open practice pavilion, leaned against a fence and watched Elena Rybakina complete the victory that ended her 99-week reign at No. 1.

ESPN captured Sabalenka viewing the final points of Rybakina's 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 quarterfinal victory over Zheng Qinwen.

There was no dramatic display. Sabalenka watched quietly, appeared to offer a small, knowing smile and then returned to work.

"Nothing she could do about it," ESPN analyst Chris Evert said during the broadcast.

It was a strikingly ordinary end to an extraordinary run.

Rybakina entered the quarterfinal needing one more victory to guarantee that she would pass Sabalenka when the WTA rankings update Monday.

Sabalenka could not influence the outcome. She had already secured her semifinal place by surviving Linda Noskova in three sets Tuesday. Even winning a third consecutive U.S. Open title would not provide enough points to remain No. 1.

Rybakina will have at least 8,681 ranking points Monday, while Sabalenka can finish with no more than 8,575, even if she successfully defends her championship.

Sabalenka stopped her practice session to watch Rybakina close out the match, then resumed preparing for Jessica Pegula.

The scene offered no evidence of anger, only recognition. Sabalenka understood exactly what Rybakina's final service hold meant.

Her uninterrupted reign, which began in October 2024, was over.

Rybakina overcame a slow, tense opening set against Zheng before taking control. She finished with 20 winners and earned the decisive break at 4-all in the third set when Zheng double-faulted.

The victory sent Rybakina into her first U.S. Open semifinal and made her the 30th woman to reach No. 1 since the WTA rankings began in 1975. She is also the first player representing Kazakhstan, male or female, to occupy the top ranking.

"It's just a number right now," Rybakina said afterward, emphasizing that she remained focused on winning the tournament.

The understated response mirrored Sabalenka's reaction from across the grounds. One player had reached the summit. The other had been displaced. Both still had matches to play.

Losing No. 1 does not eliminate Sabalenka's chance to leave New York with the trophy.

The four-time major champion will face Pegula in one semifinal, while Rybakina meets 2023 U.S. Open champion Coco Gauff in the other. A Sabalenka-Rybakina final would extend a rivalry that has already shaped the season.

Rybakina defeated Sabalenka in the Australian Open final to capture her second major title. Sabalenka responded by beating her at Indian Wells and Miami.

Now Rybakina has taken the ranking Sabalenka held for nearly two years.

The ESPN cameras preserved the precise moment Sabalenka absorbed that reality. She did not linger. She turned from the television and went back to practice, still chasing the only prize available in New York that could matter more.

title: Barry Melrose, longtime ESPN analyst former Cincinnati Stingers player, dies
description: Barry Melrose, was a longtime ESPN analyst before his Parkinson's disease diagnosis. He joined the Cincinnati Stingers of the World Hockey Association in the 1976-77 season.
fullText:
Barry Melrose, the former NHL coach who starred as an ESPN hockey analyst, has died at age 70, the network reported.

Melrose had retired from his broadcasting duties in 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.

"I've had over 50 extraordinary years playing, coaching and analyzing the world's greatest game, hockey. It's now time to hang up my skates and focus on my health, my family, including my supportive wife Cindy, and whatever comes next," Melrose said in a statement at the time.

"I'm beyond grateful for my hockey career, and to have called ESPN home for almost 30 years. Thanks for the incredible memories and I'll now be cheering for you from the stands."

Melrose, a defenseman, played in the NHL and World Hockey Association and went into coaching after his retirement.

Melrose joined the Cincinnati Stingers of the World Hockey Association for the 1976-77 season, and played for them until the league ceased operations after the 1978-79 season.

His 178 games played ranks eighth in Stingers' history. His 343 penalties minutes is second in club history, including a single-season record of 222 in 1978-79.

After stints in the Western Hockey League and American Hockey League, he began coaching the Los Angeles Kings in 1992 and took the Wayne Gretzky-led team to the Stanley Cup Final in his first season. The Kings lost to the Montreal Canadiens in five games in that series.

He coached the Kings for another two seasons and was fired in the third season. He also briefly coached the Tampa Bay Lightning in 2008-09.

Between the coaching stints, he was a popular ESPN studio analyst noted for his observations and his trademark mullet.

"Barry was my best friend at ESPN," John Buccigross posted on X. "A big brother figure of rock solid values. I am shook to my core. Barry gave his life to hockey and some of his ESPN family, like me, learned of his shocking death today while at a hockey rink in Las Vegas preparing for the upcoming season. Chilling and fitting--the rink was Barry's home. A more beloved ESPN institution there has not been. We love you, Barry. Forever."

title: Benn 'dragged down to pits of hell' by weight cut
description: Conor Benn says making the welterweight limit for his world-title challenge against Ryan Garcia has felt like being "dragged down to the pits of hell" but insists he is healthy and will make weight.
fullText:
Conor Benn says making the welterweight limit for his world title challenge against Ryan Garcia has felt like being "dragged down to the pits of hell" but insists he is healthy and will make weight.

Benn, 29, faces WBC champion Garcia at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Saturday in the first world title fight of his 10-year professional career.

The Briton must weigh no more than 10st 7lb (67kg) when he steps on the scales in on Friday, having not made the welterweight limit for more than four years.

"It's been extremely difficult," Benn told BBC Sport.

"It feels like I've been dragged down to the pits of hell, had a fight with Satan and God brought me back to life.

"Making weight has been the hardest thing I've done. I haven't made weight for four and a half years so it's going to be hard.

"But I won't moan when I'm getting paid a fortune to headline in Vegas for a world title. I know what I signed up for."

Benn last made the welterweight limit when stopping Chris van Heerden in two rounds in April 2022.

He stepped up to 11st 6lb (73kg) for two lucrative contests with Chris Eubank Jr last year, suffering the first defeat of his professional career in April 2025 before avenging the loss on points seven months later.

Benn's appearance in pictures and videos posted on social media during fight week has prompted concern among some observers over the effects of dropping back to welterweight.

Former world champion Carl Froch and Benn's former opponent Chris Algieri are among those to have questioned whether the weight cut could leave him depleted.

It is particularly pertinent given the contrasting styles on Saturday. Benn is an aggressive, front-foot fighter who likes to apply pressure, while American Garcia, 28, possesses fast hands and is renowned for a dangerous counter left hook.

But Benn dismissed concerns over his condition.

"I'm healthy," he said, adding that he expects to rehydrate significantly and enter the ring at around 12st 7lb (80kg) - two stones heavier than the welterweight limit.

Even if he fulfils a lifelong ambition by winning a maiden world title and following in his father Nigel's footsteps, Benn intends to vacate the belt "straight away" and move back up to middleweight or potentially as high as super-middleweight.

"I love challenges and that's what life is about, otherwise it's boring," he added.

For all the difficulty presented by the weight cut, there was little outward sign of Benn being weighed down by the occasion.

He was relaxed and in good spirits as he made time for the travelling British media at the UFC's Meta Apex, with father and British boxing great Nigel Benn by his side.

The former two-weight world champion has been a prominent presence throughout fight week, despite previously suggesting he would take a step back from his son's career.

One man Conor Benn is yet to see, however, is his opponent.

Garcia did not appear for a scheduled face-off at Mandalay Bay on Tuesday, with Benn told beforehand that the champion would not be attending.

Benn turned up regardless and jokingly squared up to his 62-year-old father instead.

He described Garcia as a "strange geezer" and said the no-show had done the champion "no favours".

"I'm not bothered, I've dealt with worse," Conor Benn added. "If he turns up or not, it makes no difference to me.

"Irrespective of how hard the weight cut is or anything else, we owe it to the public to give the fans what they want. It's a lack of discipline and professionalism."

fullText:
World number two Mark Selby progressed to the third round of the English Open by winning a deciding frame against China's Zhang Anda.

Zhang had levelled the tie at 3-3 with a century break, after Selby has turned round a 2-1 deficit to lead 3-2.

The 43-year-old will now meet Kyren Wilson, who won 4-3 against Wuhan Open champion Chang Bingyu, in the last 16 in Brentwood.

Oliver Lines, who defeated world number one Zhao Xintong in the first round, exited the competition with a 4-3 defeat to Yuan Sijun, losing the last two frames having pulled back from 2-0 down to lead 3-2.

World number three Judd Trump moved into the third round with a 4-1 win over Ashley Carty and will play Anthony McGill, who defeated Fan Zhengyi 4-1.

Barry Hawkins beat Daniel Wells 4-1 to set-up a tie with Mark Williams, who triumphed 4-3 over Matthew Selt, while Wu Yize sealed a 4-2 victory over compatriot Xu Si and will now face Liam Davies, who took a 4-1 win against Xinbo Wang.

title: Gauff saves match points to set up Rybakina semi-final
description: Coco Gauff saves two match points to beat Mirra Andreeva and set up a US Open semi-final against incoming world number one Elena Rybakina.
fullText:
Coco Gauff saved two match points as she fought from a set down to beat Mirra Andreeva and set up a US Open semi-final against incoming world number one Elena Rybakina.

Blown away in a 26-minute opening set, fourth seed Gauff was twice pegged back from a break up in a scrappy second set before coming through a 16-point tie-break to force a decider.

Roared on by a partisan crowd, the American's resilience proved the difference in what became a mental battle as she closed out a 2-6 7-6 (9-7) 6-2 win – a performance she said was inspired by compatriot Frances Tiafoe's comeback victory over Alex Michelsen on Tuesday night.

Progression to the last four marks back-to-back Grand Slam semi-finals for the two-time major champion and her first in New York since winning the title in 2023.

It is the first time the top four seeds have reached the semi-finals of the women's singles at a major since Wimbledon in 2009, after top seed Sabalenka and third seed Jessica Pegula progressed on Tuesday.

"At the end of the first set I was thinking about Frances and how he came back yesterday," Gauff said.

"We all want to do well in front of this crowd. Honestly, I was just trying to leave the court with no regrets."

Gauff also drew strength from her home crowd, something she has learned to embrace having struggled with the pressure of "disappointing" them with a "bad match" earlier in her career.

"I don't have that fear of disappointing them. I'm just using them and knowing that when I step on this court, they're still going to have my back," she said.

Earlier, second seed Rybakina recovered from losing a set for the first time this tournament - and going break-point down in the decider - to beat Zheng Qinwen 3-6 6-1 6-4.

The 27-year arrived at the US Open trailing Aryna Sabalenka by just 434 points and was guaranteed to secure the number one ranking for the first time in her career by reaching the semi-finals.

'Just a number' - Rybakina's rise to world number one

Rybakina reaches #1 as Gauff completes epic semis line-up

This was an uncharacteristic performance from Gauff, whose 22 winners were vastly outnumbered by 42 unforced errors, including 12 double faults.

She won just five of the opening 21 points as Andreeva breezed into a one-set lead and later failed to consolidate breaks at 4-2 and 5-3 in the second set.

A double fault at the beginning of the tie-break felt ominous, but the 22-year-old maintained her composure to save two match points - something which proved a turning point as she dominated the clutch moments in the decider.

Her response was in stark contrast to Andreeva, who struck 14 unforced errors to Gauff's two in the final set and flung a racquet in frustration following the first break of serve.

"You have to admire how Coco does this. She's done it so many times in her career," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"She's unrecognisable from the player at the start of this match. She was subdued and playing defensive tennis. By the end, she was completely controlling the match.

"We've been blessed with the amount of intriguing matches we've had. You're seeing these warriors out on court.

"It's the ability of one of the gladiators to get themselves back in it."

Addressing her outburst, Andreeva said: "I felt like I was holding my emotions for too long, not reacting on a lot of points. At one point I felt like needed to let it out."

Rybakina's ascension to the top of the rankings – the first Kazakhstani man or woman to do so – will rightly dominate the headlines.

She has achieved one of her two goals for the tournament and is now just two wins away from a second major title of the season, having won the Australian Open in January.

However, beaten opponent Zheng's achievements should not go unnoticed, offering a welcome reminder of her talent with an entertaining run to the last eight.

Having dropped out of the top 100 following elbow surgery in July 2025, the reigning Olympic champion navigated three qualifying rounds before registering her first Grand Slam main-draw win since last year's French Open.

She later stunned 22nd seed Madison Keys, who she trailed 5-0 in the third set and saved match point, and eighth seed Iga Swiatek to reach her third quarter-final in New York.

Ranked 121st heading into the tournament, she is now up to 52nd in the live rankings and has just 65 points to defend for the remainder of the season.

But for all the positives, there is an unshakable sense of what might have been against Rybakina.

Momentum was with the 23-year-old after she broke late in the first set before staving off five break points to take a 1-0 lead. However, she was completely blown away in the second set, with her second serve coming under considerable pressure.

She earned a break point in the eighth game of the decider but missed a routine backhand pass. In the next game, she brilliantly fought back from 0-40 to deuce but then followed a loose backhand with a double fault as her hopes of a maiden US Open semi-final slipped away.

description: Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembélé scored titleholder Paris Saint-Germain's first goals of the new Champions League campaign, and his first goals the season, when he netted twice in the first half against Slovan Bratislava on Wednesday.  It was a welcome return to form for Dembélé, one of France's World Cup stars with six goals, following a frustrating start to the domestic season.
fullText:
PARIS (AP) — Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembélé scored titleholder Paris Saint-Germain's first goals of the new Champions League campaign, and his first goals the season, when he netted twice in the first half against Slovan Bratislava on Wednesday.

He also set up a goal for new signing Ferran Torres as PSG led 3-0 at the break.

It was a welcome return to form for Dembélé, one of France's World Cup stars with six goals, following a frustrating start to the domestic season.

He was taken off at halftime in PSG's Ligue 1 opener after a lackluster performance against Rennes in a 2-2 draw, and was then left out of the next game against Lille by coach Luis Enrique. Dembélé was ineffective as a late second-half substitute in a 2-1 home loss to Monaco last Friday.

Dembélé put PSG ahead in the 17th minute against Slovan, reacting quickly after Nuno Mendes' swerving shot hit the post and steering the rebound inside the right post.

He clipped a shot wide from just inside the left of the penalty area moments later, before heading in his second goal in the 23rd from 18-year-old midfielder Dro Fernandez's right-wing cross.

Dembélé then set up Torres, who drifted in to meet his cross from the right for his third goal since joining from Barcelona, after scoring the winner in the World Cup final for Spain.

Dembélé dropped to his knees in frustration when he somehow hit the crossbar from close range on the half-hour mark as PSG sliced Slovan apart. Ten PSG players were nominated Tuesday on the shortlist of 30 for the Ballon d'Or, which Dembélé won for the first time last year.

Before facing Slovan at Parc des Princes, PSG had failed to win its previous four games, conceding seven goals and losing the French Super Cup to Lens.

As Bradley Barcola started in attack for new club Liverpool, his replacement Maghnes Akliouche took the field for PSG alongside Torres and Dembélé.

Another star of PSG's Champions League-winning campaign last season, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, was on the bench, as Luis Enrique fine-tunes his attack following the departures of Barcola and striker Gonçalo Ramos to AC Milan.

title: Hermann equals ODI debut score record in SA win
description: Jordan Hermann strikes 150 to equal the record for the highest score in a one-day international debut as South Africa beat Namibia by 99 runs in Windhoek.
fullText:
First one-day international, Windhoek

South Africa 348-6 (50 overs): Hermann 150 (126), De Zorzi 72 (84); Trumpelmann 4-68

Nambia 162-8 (31 overs): Kruger 34 (60); Subrayen 4-29

South Africa won by 99 runs (DLS method) and lead the three-match series 1-0

Jordan Hermann struck 150 to equal the record for the highest score in a one-day international debut as South Africa beat Namibia by 99 runs in Windhoek.

The opener's 126-ball innings saw him draw level with compatriot Matthew Breetzke, who scored 150 from 148 deliveries against New Zealand in February 2025.

Hermann put on a 167-ball second-wicket partnership of 190 with Tony de Zorzi (70), hitting 17 fours and three sixes across his innings.

The 24-year-old reached his first fifty off 61 balls but his next two half-centuries came off 32 deliveries apiece.

Having reached 150 with a single in the covers, he was dismissed from the following delivery, caught at deep-midwicket by Louren Steenkamp off the bowling of seamer Ruben Trumpelmann (4-68) to leave his side on 275-3 in the 42nd over.

South Africa added a further 73 runs to finish on 348-6 having been put into bat but lost Jordan's older brother Ruben, playing in his second ODI, for eight when he trapped lbw by Trumpelmann.

Nambia's chase was affected by rain delays and was ultimately reduced to 31 overs, with the hosts falling well short of their target of 262, revised by the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern method.

They closed on 162-8, with opener Malan Kruger top-scoring with 34, while South Africa spinner Prenelan Subrayen finished with figures of 4-29.

South Africa's win, in the first ODI encounter between the neighbouring countries, sees them go 1-0 up in the three-matches series with further fixtures to follow at the same ground on Friday and Sunday (both 08:30 BST).

The visitors have named a rotated squad for the series, with Hermann, who has made six T20 appearances for South Africa, one of three debutants in this match alongside Connor Esterhuizen and Duan Jansen.

The reserve-heavy line-up won four of their five matches in a T20 tri-series against Namibia and Zimbabwe that preceded the ODIs, with Hermann playing every fixture alongside Ruben and top-scoring with 53 in Sunday's final.

He has not been selected for South Africa's next assignment, a home series of three ODIs and three Tests against Australia, starting later this month.

title: 'Just a number' - Rybakina's rise to world number one
description: Elena Rybakina becomes the new women's world number one after reaching the US Open semi-finals, ending Aryna Sabalenka's 99-week reign at the top of the rankings.
fullText:
After 99 weeks, there will be a new women's world number one - and it will be Elena Rybakina.

Rybakina confirmed she will replace Aryna Sabalenka at the top of the world rankings on Monday with her US Open quarter-final victory over China's Zheng Qinwen.

Despite losing a set for the first time in the tournament, Rybakina fought back and saved a break point in the deciding set to complete a 3-6 6-1 6-4 win.

She is the first Kazakhstani man or woman to reach the top of the singles standings.

Rybakina has been in hot pursuit of Sabalenka this season and arrived in New York as one of three women who threatened the Belarusian's position, alongside Americans Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff.

However, the other three contenders each needed to win the title and hope Rybakina exited before the semi-finals to capture the number one spot.

Sabalenka's consecutive 99-week reign as world number one stretches back to 21 October 2024 and stands as the sixth-longest streak in WTA history.

The top two players could yet meet in the US Open final - just as they did at this year's Australian Open, where Rybakina prevailed in three sets.

For Rybakina, the trophy is more important than her new ranking.

"It's just a number right now. My goal is to win the tournaments which I play," the 27-year-old sad.

"It's an amazing achievement, but you know how quickly everything can change in tennis ranking-wise."

Rybakina will face either Coco Gauff or Mirra Andreeva in Thursday's semi-finals, while Sabalenka takes on Jessica Pegula.

Shelton beats Alcaraz in late-night 'war' to reach semis

Rybakina's push for the world number one ranking started at the end of 2025.

After losing to Sabalenka in the quarter-finals of the Wuhan Open last October, Rybakina clinched the Ningbo Open title one week later before taking her revenge by beating Sabalenka to win the season-ending WTA Finals.

She carried that momentum into 2026, getting the better of Sabalenka again but this time in a major final. She beat her fellow big-server in three competitive sets to win the Australian Open - her second Slam title almost four years after her first at Wimbledon.

Since then, Sabalenka has come out on top in their Indian Wells final and Miami Open semi-final, but Rybakina took the Stuttgart title on clay as Sabalenka's form fluctuated.

After disappointing early exits at the French Open and Wimbledon, she reached the final in Toronto, losing in straight sets to Iga Swiatek.

Rybakina's bid to replace Sabalenka suffered another setback when she was forced to retire injured from her Cincinnati Open quarter-final against Swiatek last month.

Rybakina later revealed that the left ankle problem, which hindered her movement and prevented her pushing off properly when serving, had been "bothering me for a long period of time" but was something she felt she had "under control".

Speaking before the US Open, Rybakina admitted her preparation "wasn't great" as she was unable to train for much of the week leading into the tournament.

However, that has not stopped her from achieving the first of her two major goals in New York.

Rybakina's rise to world number one has coincided with one of the most consistent periods of her career.

Despite managing her ankle injury in the lead-up to the US Open, Rybakina has backed up a 78-match 2025 season by playing 60 times so far this year.

She has won 47 of those matches, a tally bettered only by American world number three Pegula (50) on the WTA Tour.

Only Pegula can match her tally of 34 wins on hard courts this season.

But Rybakina has also won the majority of her matches against the tour's other leading players, winning 13 of her 20 meetings with fellow top-20 players.

Undoubtedly Rybakina's biggest weapon is her powerful serve.

She has recorded the most aces on the WTA Tour this year, with her total standing at 394 in 2026.

Rybakina's serve was at its devastating best against Naomi Osaka in the fourth round - she won 87% of her first-serve points and fired in seven aces among her 29 winners, but limited her unforced errors to 17.

Speaking after the match, Osaka said: "The immediate thought that I had in my head when she hit the ace, I was, like, 'well, I can't really do anything about it'."

"Maybe I could have covered it, but she has a great serve, so she probably would have hit the other way."

Rybakina has worked with coach Stefano Vukov for almost seven years.

The pair first worked together from 2019 to 2025 before splitting. Later that year Vukov was banned from the WTA Tour for breaching its code of conduct, following an independent investigation into his behaviour towards Rybakina.

Vukov, who has coached Rybakina since she was a teenager, denied any wrongdoing, and Rybakina said she was never mistreated by him.

Rybakina sought his return to her team at the start of 2025. The Croat successfully appealed the suspension and began working with Rybakina again in August last year.

She reached the US Open fourth round for the first time in her career at her first tournament since reuniting with Vukov, before embarking on the strong end-of-season form which has now propelled her to the pinnacle of the sport.

fullText:
Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable

Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? 
In August 2009, at the very first Gamescom expo, I sat in a small meeting room in Germany and played Mario Kart and World of Warcraft on a laptop, via technology that was then completely new: cloud gaming. It was a demonstration for a yet-to-be-launched service called Gaikai that promised to let you play any game in a browser window, without a console. (Here is an ancient video of that demonstration, featuring a very young Keza.) With a single click I could launch into any game, hosted on servers hundreds of miles away. It really did look like the future.

Since then, plenty of companies have tried to be the first to truly crack game streaming, vying to be the Netflix of games. Sony ended up buying Gaikai for $380m (£242m) in 2012; its technology now powers the streamable classic games library on PlayStation, and the PS5’s advanced game streaming. OnLive, Gaikai’s first competitor, launched in 2011 but shut down after less than a year, leaving Sony to acquire all its patents. Google’s Stadia cloud gaming service also imploded, launching in 2019 and shutting down three years later.

Despite the fact that people simply don’t seem to want game streaming services – or at least not enough to pay a stand-alone monthly subscription for them – Sony and Microsoft have remained steadfastly committed to the idea, bundling game streaming into their PlayStation Plus and Xbox Game Pass services. I use both quite regularly when I want to check out a game quickly, mostly because modern download sizes are ridiculous (Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, say, takes up nearly 150GB of my PS5 space, almost a quarter of its usable storage). Who wants to do 30 minutes of hard drive management every time they want to play something new?

Last week, however, Microsoft announced that it was introducing time limits for game streaming: you’re now allowed 5-15 hours a month, depending on your subscription tier. And yes, you’re right: that is not enough time to play through even one single average-sized game. This brings Microsoft’s previously unwavering commitment to cloud gaming into question – and when even Microsoft with its infinite resources can’t seem to make it work, is the writing on the wall for game streaming as a whole?

In the early days, the biggest problem with streaming was input lag: the time it took for the game to respond to your button-pressing. Normally, when you’re playing a game this lag is imperceptible. Via streaming, it would often be horribly obvious, your character taking maybe a full second to jump after you’d pressed the A button. Not all games rely heavily on timing and finesse, but a lot of them do, and playing games on a minor time-delay felt nauseating.

This is much less of an issue now, but another problem has only gotten worse: game streaming requires the instantaneous transmission of a lot of data, making it taxing on your internet connection and expensive for the service provider. Here’s a comparison: watching an hour of Netflix uses about 1GB of data. An hour of game streaming via Xbox requires about 4GB. Microsoft’s servers have to stream you the video of your live gameplay, and continually receive and interpret your controller inputs. No wonder Microsoft suddenly wants to limit your hours.

The cloud gaming model has always been based on the idea that data infrastructure would become faster and cheaper in the future. Its selling point is outsourcing computing power so that you can play whatever you want without upgrading your console or PC, or even without having one at all. Unfortunately, thanks to AI companies and their chatbots’ bottomless demand for computing power and energy, the opposite has happened. Data and computing power are now more expensive. Ironically, this change has been driven by Microsoft itself as much as anything else: a huge chunk of the company’s spending went on data centres and AI infrastructure in the last fiscal year. This suggests that Microsoft is choosing to prioritise data provision for users of Azure and Copilot over its gaming customers.

Will this affect you? Probably not. Only 4% of all Game Pass subscribers use it for more than 15 hours a month, Microsoft said in a blog post announcing the changes. Which brings us right back to the question: if cloud gaming really is the future, why is nobody using it? It’s been a long time since that 2009 demo, and this technology has still yet to meaningfully break through. Is it time to give up on it?

Alongside Sony and Microsoft, there is one other player left in this death match: the US-based tech firm Nvidia, whose GeForce Now game-streaming service (launched in 2013 and revamped many times since) might just be the world’s most successful. Nvidia has been riding high on the AI boom, becoming the most valuable company in the world. Its computing hardware powers all the datacentres that the rest of the tech industry has been building, to satisfy imagined future AI demand. Perhaps, when all of this shakes out, it will be the only company left that can afford to provide game streaming services at all.

I have been variably unwell for most of the summer, and in need of something absorbing, so I dived into Kingdom Come Deliverance II – think Skyrim, but 15th-century historical fiction.

I was impressed immediately by the outstanding script, story and performances, all of which are much more humorous and entertaining than I was expecting from a hardcore medieval RPG. And I also love how unashamedly laborious this game is: you must control each swipe of a drawn-out sword fight; you have to manually grind and mix herbs for health-restoring concoctions; and if you want anyone to speak to you, you must regularly wash your face (and grubby tunic) so you don’t stink. Last night, I spent 20 minutes hammering out horseshoes in the forge. The opening hours have you hauling sacks of flour around while a tavern landlady swears at you.

I can’t help but respect this naturalist commitment to grime and busywork; knight-life isn’t all horseplay, you know. I have spent many, many hours with this game and I am still basically a stinking peasant. I may well never finish it, but I am resolved to at least get to the point where I have my own steed and a pair of decent boots.

Available on: Xbox, PlayStation 5, PC

 Estimated playtime: 55+ hours

A Nintendo broadcast on Tuesday spilled a bunch of new details about the upcoming Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, which I’m relieved to say is looking beautiful. Link looks doll-like in the updated style, and Hyrule Castle Town looks a bit like a living Playmobil village overlaid with a watercolour-ish filter that makes the whole game look like something half remembered. (I am somewhat less enthused by the addition of voice acting to the cutscenes; Navi was already annoying enough.) Check out the demo here.

For the Ringer, frequent Guardian games contributor Lewis Gordon has written this excellent long-read on Japanese publisher Capcom’s current streak of brilliance, talking to a host of executives and developers about exactly how the company has bucked the trend while the rest of the games industry is on fire.

Patrick Miller – better known as pattheflip – has published a thought-provoking reflection on how and why some players become overinvested – even dependent – on video games. “I say this as someone who has loved video games his whole life; if games serve a load-bearing function in someone’s life, it’s the life that needs fixing, not the games.”

At the end of last week, the White House released this horrible little propaganda arcade, featuring nasty riffs on popular games, such as a version of Tetris where you have to build a wall on the Mexican border to stave off “the coming horde”. That particular game was later removed after The Tetris Company expressed its opposition.

Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar

‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged world

Reader Piero sent in this question (along with some super-nice feedback on the newsletter – thank you, Piero!):

“I enjoy the occasional foray into story-driven RPGs, such as Kingdom Come Deliverance, Skyrim and the Baldur’s Gate series, but as I get older I’m finding the continual combat sections overwhelming and dull. Could you recommend me some good RPGs that don’t rely on combat as the main game mechanic?”

You’re not alone, Piero – for a surprising proportion of players, combat is just something you have to do in order to get to the bits of a game that you find more interesting. Most RPGs these days have a “story mode” option that at least makes all the fighting trivially easy, if you’re not interested in engaging with it. There is of course Disco Elysium, a complex role-playing game with no combat at all; like Citizen Sleeper, it is mostly text-based. I have heard good things about Eastshade, an open-world game where you’re a painter rather than a fighter. I’d also suggest Pentiment, though it’s a very different style from Skyrim. And Yonder: The Cloud Catcher Chronicles is worth a look if you don’t mind cutesy.

title: Kimi Raikkonen's son Robin, 11, signs for Red Bull
description: Robin Raikkonen, the 11-year-old son of former Formula 1 world champion Kimi Raikkonen, signs for Red Bull's driver development programme.
fullText:
Robin Raikkonen, the 11-year-old son of former Formula 1 world champion Kimi Raikkonen, has signed for Red Bull.

Nicknamed 'Ace', the youngster has impressed in karting championships and will join Red Bull's driver development programme in 2027.

The programme has produced F1 drivers such as Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen - both four-time champions.

Robin's father, nicknamed 'Iceman', was the most recent Ferrari driver to become world champion, claiming his sole title in 2007.

The Finn claimed 21 wins and 103 podiums from 349 F1 starts before retiring in 2021. He also competed in the World Rally Championship and Nascar.

"We are all thrilled and excited that Robin has been chosen to further his racing path as a member of the Red Bull junior team," said 46-year-old Kimi.

"They offer a compelling and comprehensive programme to develop and nurture Robin's progress over the coming years and provide him with all the experience required to develop his natural talent."

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said Robin has "already demonstrated exceptional ability in karting".

"His speed, racecraft and natural talent have established him as one of the most promising young drivers in his age group," Mekies added.

"At the same time, he impresses with his maturity, his calm approach and his clear focus on driving.

"Our goal is to develop him step by step, without placing any unnecessary pressure on his shoulders.

"The path through motorsport is a long one and we will give him the time, support and resources he needs to maximise his potential."

Robin follows in the footsteps of Ella Hakkinen, the daughter of Finland's double world champion Mika Hakkinen, who joined McLaren's driver development programme last year.

A NYC firehouse was first to respond on 9/11. 25 years on, Sal Argano is the last still on staff
description: Sal Argano got lucky.  When the World Trade Center was struck by hijacked jets on Sept. 11, 2001, the New York City firefighter was in Brooklyn, on loan to another station, rather than at his usual po...
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — Sal Argano got lucky. When the World Trade Center was struck by hijacked jets on Sept. 11, 2001, the New York City firefighter was in Brooklyn, on loan to another station, rather than at his usual post at the small Manhattan firehouse just across an intersection from the twin towers.

He rushed downtown to find his firehouse badly damaged but still standing. Six of its members, he'd later learn, were among the 343 New York City firefighters killed in the World Trade Center's collapse.

"If I wasn't sent out on rotation there would have been a good chance I would not be here today," Argano says. "I think about that all the time."

Almost 25 years later, Argano, now 65, is still on duty at the firehouse — the last of the firefighters assigned there in 2001 who still works there.

Today, the crews at the firehouse respond to emergency calls but also serve as a de facto part of the 9/11 memorial, visited by crowds of tourists daily.

Some visitors come specifically to see the large bronze relief along the side of the building listing the names of the firefighters killed on 9/11.

Others pause to take selfies as they pass by on their way to the National 9/11 Memorial plaza across the street, drawn by the sight of Engine 10 and Ladder 10, the gleaming trucks sitting in the garage that give the station its nickname: Ten House.

"This is definitely one of those companies where if you don't want to ingratiate yourself to the public, it's definitely not the right place," said Capt. Terence Brody, who commands Ladder 10 and has worked at the station since 2016. "People around the world know this firehouse. They're going to come by and say hello."

Brody, now 55, was still in the fire academy on 9/11. Cadets grabbed their gear and were bused to ground zero.

The debris hung so thickly in the air around the fallen towers that it looked like it was snowing, he said.

"It was a beautiful sunny Tuesday, and then you're in this kind of apocalyptic atmosphere," Brody said. "It was a little overwhelming, to say the least."

In the days after the attack, Ten House served as both command center and safe space for weary first responders, he said. As the years passed, its crew had a front-row seat to the area's rebirth.

Robert Favata joined Ladder 10 in 2008, fresh out of the academy.

In those early years, he worked beside a giant hole teeming with construction activity. Now 46, he looks out at a transformed landscape.

A pair of waterfall pools sit in the footprint of the old towers, ringed by parapets etched with the names of nearly 3,000 victims. Below ground, the 9/11 Museum houses mangled steel beams, a destroyed fire truck and other artifacts. New skyscrapers ring the memorial.

"When I got here, there was nothing," Favata says. "I never thought they were gonna finish."

Argano can be found most days perched near the station's open bay doors, patiently answering questions, shaking hands and posing for photos.

He says Ten House firefighters have a unique charge: they're both living testimonials to the events of 9/11 as well as public faces of the centuries-old FDNY.

Argano says he tries to impress on younger firefighters — many increasingly not even born before the attacks — the importance of treating every visitor with respect.

"This is not like any other firehouse," he said. "We have our fire duty, we have our responses, and then we have a responsibility toward the people outside."

He acknowledges the task is not always easy. The packs of gawking tourists can be relentless. Their questions can sometimes come across too personal, too insincere or just simply too out there.

Many of the younger firefighters tend to keep a lower profile for that reason, he said.

After responding to an early morning call this particular day, most of the crew heads to the back of the station to stow their gear or upstairs to help prepare lunch.

Argano meanwhile chats up a firefighter from France and his wife and then invites them into the station.

He points to a wall of patches from fire departments across the world that have been gifted over the years, as well as the well-worn helmets hanging in the rafters.

At another point, though, a lady asks — perhaps a bit too flippantly — what's so special about Ten House.

Argano shrugs: "It's just a fire station." After she departs, he says it simply wasn't worth the effort.

"If I need to explain to you all of that, then it's like, 'Pull up a seat'," Argano said. "Let me get another cigarette. It's gonna be a long one."

Favata considers the approaching 25th anniversary as likely one of his last before retirement. He worries, though, if he's done enough to keep the memories of Ten House alive.

"When I got here, so many of the guys worked 9/11 and they told me their stories of that day," Favata said, choking on tears. "I just hope I can give like a percentage of what they've told me to the younger guys."

Brody, meanwhile, handed in his retirement papers Tuesday. His last day will be in October.

"It's interesting to think that my first day in the field was right across the street, and this is where I'm gonna end my career," said Brody, who writes screenplays in his spare time and has already had two of them turned into Hallmark Channel movies.

But Argano, who drives Engine 10, isn't quite ready to pack it in. He fears something will be lost when no one is there who still remembers.

"I'm not done. I'm gonna be here as long as I can," Argano said. "I'm going to keep telling them what I know, what I saw, what I've been through. Telling them the history of this firehouse. Everything I can remember."

title: England to extend head coach Borthwick's contract
description: England head coach Steve Borthwick will have his contract extended past the 2028 Six Nations in a bid to avoid uncertainty over his future before and during next year's Rugby World Cup.
fullText:
England head coach Steve Borthwick will have his contract extended past the 2028 Six Nations in a bid to avoid uncertainty over his future before and during next year's Rugby World Cup.

As it did with Red Roses boss John Mitchell before the 2025 World Cup, the Rugby Football Union has moved to ensure Borthwick and his staff have some clarity over their positions going into the global showpiece.

According to RFU performance director Conor O'Shea, extending Borthwick's deal into the middle of 2028 will allow time to decide who leads the team in the longer-term.

"You don't want them looking for a job going into [a World Cup]," O'Shea explained.

"Everyone knows it will be judged on the World Cup, but you can't have a group of coaches going in with that uncertainty, especially when you look at the timing.

"So we will give that certainty, and that will give us time to look properly."

In a wide-ranging interview on the Rugby Union Weekly podcast, O'Shea discussed:

England's prospects next year, with O'Shea believing England are one of five teams who can win the 2027 World Cup

the RFU's stringent selection rules for England players, with O'Shea saying the unintended consequences of picking players based overseas would be "massive"

the succession plan for Red Roses boss Mitchell and how O'Shea doesn't feel the England women's side can ever be too strong despite their four-year dominance of the world game.

Conor O'Shea: Borthwick's contract, overseas rule & Red Roses

Following a review into England's "horrendous" Six Nations earlier this year, Borthwick has been backed to lead the team through to the World Cup, with O'Shea adding he can't see a scenario where Borthwick isn't in charge in Australia.

In the July leg of the Nations Championship, England recovered from a bruising defeat by South Africa in Johannesburg to vanquish Fiji in Liverpool and edge out Argentina to finish the campaign with two wins from three.

However at this stage the RFU has stopped short of committing to Borthwick on a long-term basis, unlike Ireland, who have signed their head coach Andy Farrell up to 2031.

"I see in Steve someone who bleeds England, and wants England to succeed more than anything you can imagine," O'Shea said.

"This England team is unequivocally one of probably five teams who can win the World Cup next year. I believe this team can win a World Cup.

"Is the talent there? 100%," he added.

"If over this next 12 months this England team shows the best version of itself, I know it can beat anyone in the world."

As was the case for a number of his predecessors, Borthwick is only able to select players based in the English Prem, meaning the likes of Toulouse flanker Jack Willis – one of the outstanding performers in the French Top 14 – is ineligible for his country.

Cap centurion Courtney Lawes, who has returned to English rugby with Sale after two seasons at Brive, believes the RFU should review the policy to ensure the best players are available.

But O'Shea is adamant the ruling is what works for English rugby as a whole, and has warned against the impact of loosening the policy.

"It is something done not just for England, but for English rugby," O'Shea said.

"As of now, if all the best players were picked by England and went abroad, and we had less of the top players in our league, the unintended consequence towards investment into that from some of our owners… why would you invest in the pathways if the best players are going to be taken away?

"I get it completely, the life experiences are great. But for the English game, it is absolutely the right thing."

England should pick English-based players - Baxter

Allow overseas stars to play for England - Lawes

Since joining the RFU in January 2020, O'Shea has overseen England women's global dominance, aided by the establishment and development of Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR).

And while the resources and player numbers at England dwarf those at many of their rivals, O'Shea rejects the notion that the Red Roses can ever be too strong.

The world champion Roses are unbeaten in four years and have won every Six Nations since 2018.

Conversely in the men's game, no nation has won three Six Nations in a row in the professional era.

"Does competitive tension create greater commercialisation and broadcast? I get all that," O'Shea said.

"But I do think when you look at the PWR, and what we have done in terms of allowing a lot of players to come over here and allow them the platform to develop as players, England plays a huge role in driving that.

"Was it bad when you had a dominant Tiger Woods, or Serena Williams? What about celebrating what they are. They have been the standard bearer."

title: Amazon Is Selling Its First Sterling Bonds in Four-Part Deal
description: Amazon.com Inc. kicked off the sale of its debut sterling bonds in a four-part deal, as hyperscalers continue to turn to global debt markets to fuel the artificial intelligence arms race.
fullText:
(Bloomberg) -- Amazon.com Inc. kicked off the sale of its debut sterling bonds in a four-part deal, as hyperscalers continue to turn to global debt markets to fuel the artificial intelligence arms race.

Apple's $2,000-Plus Foldable iPhone Was a Decade in the Making

Bessent Dares Traders to Bet Against Yen: 'I Am the House Now'

EU and Canada Plan Deal to Boost Trade, Security as US Ties Fray

Apple to Unveil $2,000 Foldable iPhone Duo at High-Stakes Event

Indonesia's Richest Family Moves More Than $1 Billion Offshore

The company is selling tranches with maturities ranging from three to 19 years, according to a person familiar with the matter. Initial price discussions are for around 70 basis points over UK gilts for the shortest to around 110 basis points for the longest, said the person, who asked not to be named.

JPMorgan Chase & Co., Barclays Plc, HSBC Holdings Plc and Natwest Group Plc are managing the deal, which is expected to be priced later on Wednesday.

The sale is Amazon's fourth outside the US dollar market so far this year. It tapped euros for the first time in March with the biggest-ever corporate deal in the currency, did a record six tranches in the Swiss franc market, as well as the largest-ever debt offering in the Canadian dollar market. Overall, it's the top bond issuer among so-called hyperscalers in 2026, having sold the equivalent of more than $92 billion in securities.

Amazon's first sterling bond "highlights the broader question for hyperscalers: how much debt can investors absorb as AI investment drives repeated issuance? The appetite remains for hundreds of billions more," said Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Robert Schiffman and Suchi Trivedi.

The company is following a similar path to Alphabet Inc., which has been around the world for new funding sources for its AI spending. The Google parent company raised £5.5 billion ($7.5 billion) of sterling debt in February, including a ultra-rare 100-year bond, pulling in nearly £30 billion in demand. Alphabet has since tapped the Australian dollar and Japanese yen markets.

The BI analysts also highlighted the sterling bond market's limited supply of large-cap technology company debt, which should support demand for Amazon's sale, though the 19-year tranche is a test of investors' willingness to extend duration for AI-linked capital needs.

Investors are starting to push back on the deluge of AI related debt. More recent sales have attracted weaker demand and priced at higher costs compared to those sold earlier in the year.

title: Highest paid world leader to get salary increase of $1M
description: Singapore's prime minister Lawrence Wong will see his annual pay rise to 3.6 million Singapore dollars ($2.8m; £2.1m).
fullText:
Singapore's government says it will raise the annual salaries of its ministers and other office holders, including its prime minister who is the highest paid political leader in the world.

Lawrence Wong will see an increase of 1.4 million Singapore dollars ($1.1m; £818,000) in his annual pay package. He has said he will donate this pay increase to charity over the next five years.

Wong said that raising the pay of ministers was necessary to attract better talent. The government has previously argued that paying ministers high salaries deters corruption.

But the move has attracted criticism in Singapore where there is deep concern about job security and the rising cost of living.

Even before his pay raise kicks in, Wong is still by far the highest paid world leader.

He currently receives an annual salary of S$2.2m and will now see his pay go up by more than 60% to S$3.6m ($2.8m).

Next is Hong Kong chief executive John Lee, who earns about $719,000, followed by Switzerland's president Guy Parmelin with $606,000.

US president Donald Trump earns $400,000 a year, while British PM Andy Burnham takes in $230,000.

On Tuesday, Wong acknowledged that Singapore ministers' salaries have attracted scrutiny given that they were much more than what most citizens earn. The median monthly income in the country is S$5,775.

But he argued that he has faced difficulty convincing business leaders and top civil servants to run for political office.

While the government cannot match what some of these people earn, "we do not make the financial hurdle unnecessarily high" for them to give up their careers and join politics, he said.

"Overall, I believe this will give me and future prime ministers a better chance of persuading capable Singaporeans to step forward, and of building the strongest possible team for Singapore," he said.

Currently, the base pay package of ministers is about S$1.1m. With the new pay scheme, that will increase to around S$1.2m.

But Wong said he expects most of these ministers to receive even more than that - around S$1.35m - by the end of the current term of government, as pay will increase based on performance.

Part of their pay package is determined by whether the country reaches certain targets for unemployment rate, income growth, and GDP growth.

The topic of high salaries for Singapore's ministers has long been a lightning rod of criticism for the ruling People's Action Party (PAP), which has led the country since independence.

In a landmark general election in 2011 the PAP saw its lowest vote share in decades, fuelled partly by voters' unhappiness over ministers' pay as well as immigration policies. The following year, the government slashed ministers' salaries.

Wong's predecessor, Lee Hsien Loong, had also pledged to donate his salary increase to charity for several years back in 2007.

The government has for years pointed to its lack of corruption - Singapore consistently ranks near the top of Transparency International's annual Corruption Perceptions Index - as proof that the ministerial pay system works, arguing that it reduces the temptation for ministers to accept bribes.

But in a country where the average income is far below such sums, the issue continues to rankle and the latest announcement is no exception.

On Tuesday many online posted comments critical of the pay raise, saying it was "tone deaf" given current concerns about retrenchments, jobs for fresh graduates and inflation.

Retrenchments in Singapore hit their highest level in more than five years in the last quarter, according to government figures.

But there were a few who agreed with the move, saying it was necessary to have "the best of the best" running the country.

title: Nicaragua tells top UN court Germany is violating international law by selling weapons to Israel
description: Nicaragua told the United Nations’ top court on Tuesday that Germany has breached the Genocide Convention by selling Israel weapons that were used in the country's war in Gaza.  Nicaragua argued that ...
fullText:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — Nicaragua told the United Nations' top court on Tuesday that Germany has breached the Genocide Convention by selling Israel weapons that were used in the country's war in Gaza.

Nicaragua argued that Germany is violating international law by "facilitating" acts of genocide in Gaza by providing arms and other military support to Israel, in proceedings at the International Court of Justice. Berlin denies the allegation.

While the case centers on Germany, it indirectly takes aim at Israel's campaign in Gaza in response to the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas. Israel, which isn't a party in the proceedings, strongly denies that its actions amount to acts of genocide. The preliminary hearings focus on whether the court has jurisdiction.

The proceedings are the latest legal attempt to rein in Israel's military campaign by a country with historic ties to the Palestinian people, after South Africa accused Israel of genocide at the same court in 2023.

"It is impossible that with the type of political, commercial and military relations of Germany with Israel, they could not be aware, or normally should have been aware, of the serious risk that acts that could amount to genocide were being committed by Israel," Nicaragua's top lawyer, Carlos José Argüello Gómez, told the court.

Germany has been a staunch supporter of Israel for decades and is the second-largest supplier of arms to Israel after the United States.

Nicaragua's government has historical links with Palestinian organizations dating back to their support for the 1979 Sandinista revolution.

On Monday, Germany told the court that the case was improperly filed and should be thrown out.

"Nicaragua's conduct indicates that it was not interested in hearing Germany's view on its allegations, but simply in bringing Germany before this court," Julia Monar, Germany's top lawyer, told the judges. Countries are typically expected to attempt to resolve disputes before bringing them to the court.

Lawyers for Nicaragua denied this, pointing to documents sent to the German foreign ministry as well as press releases describing the dispute.

The ruling on jurisdiction is expected later this year and, if Nicaragua's case moves forward, the proceedings could take years.

title: Legal action against Fifa to include women's schedule
description: Legal action from the top European leagues and global players' union Fifpro against Fifa is extended to include the world governing body's "abusive conduct" towards the women's game.
fullText:
Legal action from the top European leagues and global players' union Fifpro against Fifa has been extended to include the world governing body's "abusive conduct" towards the women's game.

European Leagues, which represents 53 professional divisions, including the Premier League, and 1,328 clubs in 34 countries, first filed the complaint to the European Commission to protect the welfare of men's players in October 2024.

The complaint stated that Fifa abused a dominant position under European competition law allegedly by not including national leagues and player unions over the new men's international calendar announced in 2023.

In a statement on Tuesday, it said it is extending the scope of its complaint to include "Fifa's abusive conduct regarding the women's international match calendar and related women's football regulatory decisions".

"Fifa's conduct threatens the growth and financial sustainability of women's professional leagues, and risks player health and wellbeing," European Leagues said.

"The European Commission must now act to ensure that EU law is respected and that the future of women's professional football is not determined unilaterally by Fifa.

"The submission details the same pattern of conduct identified in the original complaint - Fifa holds conflicting roles as governing body and competition organiser, which gives rise to a conflict of interest.

"As in men's football, Fifa consistently uses its regulatory power to favour its own competition and commercial interests to the detriment of women's football and of European national leagues."

European Leagues welcomed 14 women's divisions to its ranks in June, including the Women's Super League and the Scottish Women's Premier League.

It also includes the Premier League, English Football League, Scottish Professional Football League, La Liga, Serie A and the Bundesliga.

A Fifa spokesperson said: "Fifa believes in the power of dialogue as opposed to legal action and escalation, and our doors always remain open to reach agreements in the best interest of football.

"As a matter of fact, a landmark agreement reached with Fifpro earlier this year enabled groundbreaking reforms to the global transfer system, jointly adopted in full consensus with all football stakeholders.

"As the women's global landscape continues to grow and broaden, Fifa is committed to expand and identify emerging stakeholders in anticipation of the conversations that will begin on the next iteration of the March calendar."

Fifa president Infantino will stand for re-election

Division, drama and power - what next for Infantino and Uefa?

Fifa has been under intense scrutiny in the summer after its president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup and its other competitions to private investors.

Infantino's plan sparked a global outcry, with Uefa threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.

European football's governing body dropped the threat after receiving assurances from Fifa that the plan will not go ahead.

Infantino has been under pressure from several confederations after the scrapped Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan but the Swiss is set to stand for re-election as president in March.

The 56-year-old, who first became president in 2016, is seeking a third term in the role until 2031.

Fifa last week accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership", in a challenge to litigation over Infantino's plan.

Uefa had filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.
