title: I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AI
description:
A Dr Seuss-style story written in seconds alerted me to the power – and perils – of the technology. But how can children embrace it without forgetting core skills?
When I was growing up, my dad and I often talked about a story we wanted to write together. It was called “The Day Nobody Went to Disneyland”. One day, the story goes, the weather is so perfect that everyone in the world decides to stay away from Disneyland because they expect it to be far too busy.
fullText:
A Dr Seuss-style story written in seconds alerted me to the power – and perils – of the technology. But how can children embrace it without forgetting core skills?

When I was growing up, my dad and I often talked about a story we wanted to write together. It was called “The Day Nobody Went to Disneyland”. One day, the story goes, the weather is so perfect that everyone in the world decides to stay away from Disneyland because they expect it to be far too busy. But my dad, who has the same thought as them, sees the disappointment on my face that morning – and decides to risk it. We set off. And when we arrive, the park is completely empty. Nobody else was brave enough to visit. We have everything – the rides, shows, food – to ourselves.

I loved the idea of writing that story. But, as so often happens, we were too busy to do anything about it. Life ran away from us. I grew up, and we both forgot about it.

Thirty years later, I was at my parents’ for dinner with my own children (eight, five and two). For some reason, the idea popped into my mind again. I told my oldest about it – and she wanted to hear the full thing. We turned to ChatGPT, gave it the vague outline and asked it to have a go at writing the story in the style of Dr Seuss (one of our favourites). Within a few seconds, we had it. She read it out – and we laughed.

Of course, what this AI generated wasn’t perfect. A few lines didn’t quite make sense; a few Americanisms had slipped in (“sneakers”, “cinnamon buns”). But that night on the sofa we had great fun together tweaking the prompts, refining the story, adding more scenes, working with this strange new creative partner to do something that had escaped my grasp for decades.

For the last 15 years, I have been exploring the impact of AI on work and society. But becoming a dad of three small people has made these disruptions far more personal: it is clear that their future is going to look wildly different from my past.

For my wife, that realisation really sunk in a few weeks ago, on a journey to her parents’ in Suffolk. Three children, confined in a car, stuttering along the A12, is a combustible setup. So we were thrilled to find a rare podcast that everyone miraculously enjoyed: History’s Not Boring, a series of 15-minute bursts of conversation, on a kaleidoscope of subjects, narrated by two children.

As we listened, we started to speculate in the car about who these whiz-kids might be. Where were they from? How were they selected? How did they juggle this job with school? Eventually, I went to the website to find out. All our answers were wrong. The kids did not, in fact, exist. The entire podcast seemed to be generated by AI. None of us had realised.

It was a strange moment, learning that people we had grown fond of were not actually people at all. It was also remarkable that AI could create such high-quality educational content. But for my wife, a podcast and documentary maker, it was an unsettling moment as well: here was something that would have taken her and a talented team several days to make, and now it was being done without people.

My work on AI has taken me to boardrooms and conference halls, classrooms and government buildings. But wherever I go, one question is now asked more than any other: what should my children do?

Today, we are floundering. Teachers worry that the way they teach no longer seems to work. Parents, watching their children use AI to solve problems and answer questions, wonder what they really know. Employers doubt whether traditional educational achievements, awarded in time-honoured ways – coursework, exams, assessments – are still a useful guide to what young people can do.

Yet reacting to these new technologies by putting barriers up, as many instinctively want to do – banning, admonishing, punishing – just cannot be right. To begin with, this is the water in which the next generation will swim: we are letting them down if we prepare them for the world that we grew up in, not the one they will actually inhabit.

How often, for instance, have you heard people accuse students of cheating if they use AI to help them with their work? But at what point are we cheating them by failing to overhaul the way we are educating them? If AI is making education “too easy” for young people, at what point does the burden shift on to us, the adults, to make their education more testing, to push them on, to stretch them?

More importantly, this dismissiveness of AI is also unimaginative. It stops us appreciating the astounding possibilities AI could create for the next generation as well. Of course there are risks. But at the same time, if we use this technology wisely, what difficult ideas might the next generation now grasp, ones that were beyond us when we were in their shoes? What hard problems might they now solve, ones that once required years of training and experience – if they were solvable at all?

A big part of the challenge of AI is that our traditional response to technological disruption in the working world – the idea of “future-proofing” people – no longer works. In 2013, the then prime minister David Cameron announced that England would become the first place in the world where all children in primary and secondary schools would learn to code. This, in the words of education secretary Michael Gove, would “equip every child with the computing skills they need to succeed in the 21st century”.

The idea seemed bold and clever: in the years that followed, it was hard to find an advanced country that did not follow our example.

Fast-forward to today. What does it turn out that the latest AI systems, such as ChatGPT and Claude, are best at doing? Writing code. In January 2026, Anthropic reported that 90% of the code for Claude Code – their AI-powered coding assistant – was itself written by AI. Skills that were meant to protect kids from technological disruption for their entire lives were largely redundant before they had even left school.

For politicians and policymakers, it is tempting to dismiss the coding saga as an unfortunate blip. But this is a mistake. The reason they slipped up was because they had believed in the idea of “future-proof” skills, the thought that there exists some valuable set of skills that AI will not be able to do for some time – and that by thinking deeply enough about the future, we can accurately identify them.

The truth is that we know only two things about what lies ahead. One is that it will be full of technologies that are far more capable than today. And the other is that we know little else. But rather than attempting to resolve this uncertainty, we have to accept it and instead ask a different question: how do we prepare the next generation to flourish in a future that we actually know surprisingly little about?

The first step is to get back to basics. Since 2009, literacy and numeracy have been falling among young people around the world, according to the OECD’s programme for international student assessment (Pisa); the same holds true for adults. In itself, this is worrying. But given the uncertainty that we face about the future, these trends are a disaster.

Why such a calamity? To begin with, while it might be hard to say precisely which more advanced skills will turn out to be most valuable in the future – creativity, judgment, something else – they will rely in some way on these basic skills. They are the foundations for everything else.

What’s more, AI systems are far from flawless. They make mistakes, often on simple problems; they hallucinate, providing confident and plausible answers that are completely made up. They are, as the computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton put it, “idiot savants”. That means we must use AI critically, not blindly, keeping our basics sharp so we can tell when AI is being a savant – or an idiot.

So, with both those reasons in mind, we should be focusing intensely on teaching literacy and numeracy, even if AI does them better, as it increasingly seems to do. Getting back to basics is what an economist would call a “no-regrets” strategy – we will never regret improving these basic skills, however the future turns out to be.

And we should try to be imaginative. When my eight-year-old grew bored learning her times tables the traditional way – long lists, learned by rote – I turned to ChatGPT to create various computer games, designed by her, to test what she knew. (Unicorns and rainbows featured in all versions.)

Then there was the time my five-year-old was tired of reading his standard-issue phonics books after school – there really is only so much Biff, Chip and Kipper a human being can take – and instead we used AI to generate some custom stories together, carefully tuned to his reading level and much closer to his favourite topics. (At the time of writing, HMS Belfast, TNT explosives and Bukayo Saka.)

Experimentation is important and we can learn so much from the creativity of others. Take Chris Moran, for instance, head of editorial innovation at the Guardian. His daughter had been reading Dracula at school but was struggling to place the sprawling novel in the real world. Together, with the help of AI, they built an app – PlotLines – which placed the story on an interactive 1890s Ordnance Survey Map, plotting the key scenes and character journeys around Europe, with the help of AI. (They have done it for many other books now, too.)

These are precisely the sorts of innovations we should be testing and embracing throughout education – rather than banning.

Despite the uncertainty we face, there is still one thing that we do know about the future: it will be full of technologies that are vastly more powerful than today. With that in mind, we must teach the next generation to use them. To do this properly will require us to dedicate a serious chunk of time to teaching people how to use AI.

The challenge, though, is how to do this without also setting them up to forget crucial basic skills. An important, growing fear is that AI is making us stupid. Why bother reading a book if AI can summarise it? Why bother completing maths homework if AI will do the sums? And in my view the answer here lies not in Silicon Valley, but with a forgotten British maths professor, Wilfred Halliday Cockcroft, half a century ago.

In the 1970s, the quality of maths teaching in UK schools appeared to be collapsing and numeracy was reportedly low. Cockcroft, who had a longstanding interest in mathematics education, was asked by the government to look into it. And in 1982 the Cockcroft Report was published. It was enormous, forensic – and is now largely forgotten. But it may turn out to be the most important document written for thinking about the future of education, because of its response to the electronic calculator.

It is fascinating to read Cockcroft’s report and discover how the challenges of the calculator back then were so similar to the ones we face with AI today – from the fear that it would undermine “basic skills” to the intimidation many felt at the complexity of this strange new technology (“Some … had been discouraged by the large number of figures which had appeared after the decimal point”).

Cockcroft was realistic: “all candidates”, he expected, “will have access to a calculator by 1985”. And his proposal was revolutionary: overhauling mathematics education by splitting it into two parts, spending part of the time teaching students to use a calculator and the rest of the time learning to cope without one – and crucially, testing both. It caught on. Learning maths without and with a calculator is now the gold standard around the world, the former nurturing the basics and the latter applying them to more fiendish problems.

We should also be realistic and revolutionary, adopting this tried-and-tested principle – what I call “teach both, test both” – for AI now. Every subject, from history to English literature, should be divided in two: teach students to use AI in one part, teach students to flourish without it in the other – and, crucially, examine both. A teacher cannot monitor whether or not a student uses AI in the quiet solitude of their bedroom. But nothing can replace the feeling of sitting in an exam, looking at the paper, and feeling that cold sweat when you realise you haven’t prepared for both parts.

One of my worries is that we allow a legitimate sense of concern about the impact of social media on children’s lives to seep into how we think about AI, allowing good restrictions on the former to turn into kneejerk bans on the latter. Social media and AI are not the same thing, and whereas the former often dehumanises and distracts us from the real world, AI – used in the right way – can make our lives go far better.

There is another way to think about this: a debate is now under way about the “Goldilocks” amount of screen time for children – not too much, not too little, just the right amount. But this is not the right argument to be having. What matters is not so much the amount of screen time, but what is actually on those screens, what we are using this technology to do.

This distinction matters not only for thinking about what we teach, but how we teach as well. Consider a further example: personal tuition. It is often said an average student who receives one-to-one tuition will outperform almost all their peers in a traditional classroom setting. I saw this first-hand, as a tutor in Oxford for years, teaching mathematics and economics.

The problem, though, is that human tutors are too expensive to provide to everyone. But now, AI can finally provide high-quality personal tuition, tailoring the way material is taught to the unique strengths and weaknesses of each student, mimicking interactions with a human tutor but at a far lower cost.

In all honesty, AI provides a level of tailored instruction that I – and many other teachers I have watched over the years – have struggled to achieve. In part, it is the breadth of AI that is striking. I have used it to respond to my five-year-old’s bedtime-delaying tactic of asking vast questions just as I turn down the lights (in response to, “Daddy, where did the first human come from?” it drew up a short story about evolution), as well as to create step-by-step instructions to help graduate students solve hard mathematical problems in economics, such as the Ramsey growth model.

“I don’t think anyone has ever paid such pure attention to me and my thinking and my questions,” a student was reported as saying in The New Yorker in April 2025. “It’s made me rethink my interactions with people.” AI never gets tired or distracted. It doesn’t have fixed office hours or limited classroom time. It will always answer one more question, always provide one more explanation of a problem you don’t understand.

I am not surprised that students have been booing tech titans during recent US graduation ceremonies. The most resistant groups I have spoken to over the last 15 years are young professionals: they have spent a big chunk of their life, and sunk huge amounts of money, preparing to be a lawyer or doctor or whatever it might be, and they are understandably furious when they are told, just as they cross the finish line, that the world they were preparing to enter is over.

There is so much advice I would want to give them, worried at the start of their careers. But one of the most important bits is to choose a profession because the problem interests you, not the job. Bluntly, if you go into medicine because you like the look of doctors on House, or law because of Suits, or marketing because of Mad Men, then you are going to be disappointed. These jobs are soon going to look very different.

But the problems themselves – improving health outcomes, providing legal advice, selling products? They are not going away. It is the way we solve them, and the skills required to do so, that will look very different.

You could glimpse this well before the arrival of generative AI. Back in 2017, a team at Stanford University announced they had built a system that could tell whether or not a freckle was cancerous from a photograph as accurately as leading dermatologists. It was a remarkable moment, a lurch forward in AI-enabled diagnostics. Yet what was particularly interesting about this work is that the final co-author on the Nature article that announced this achievement was Sebastian Thrun – not a medical doctor, but a leading computer scientist who developed the world’s first driverless car. Here was a man who knew very little about medicine at all, yet with the skills that he had was able to build a system that could rival the expertise of the finest doctors.

What would I actually do if I were at the start of my career, back in the starting blocks of life? Without hesitation, I would run towards AI and science – not because it is protected from automation, but because it is where the most excitement is likely to happen in years to come. In the 20th century, the best ideas we had about the world came from the heads of clever human beings. In the 21st century, I expect they are likely to come from capable AIs instead.

We could catch a glimpse of that in late 2024, when the creators of an AI built by DeepMind – AlphaFold2 – won the Nobel prize in chemistry for solving the “protein folding problem” (one of the greatest unsolved challenges in biology, critical for understanding how diseases work and how to treat them). At the time of writing, frontier mathematics is next in line, new discoveries appearing at an impressive rate.

The more time I spend with AI, the more I realise the main constraint on its use in the world is the limits of our imagination. Even if we were to press pause on progress in the technology today, there would be vastly more uses for it than we have currently dreamed up.

Part of the imaginative task falls to us. But that night with my eight-year-old, crafting that story, reminds me that part of it falls to the next generation as well. “We look at the world once in childhood,” wrote the poet Louise Glück, “the rest is memory.” In that spirit, we need the next generation, with their sense of adventure and open-mindedness, their lack of world-weariness, to help us think wisely and freely, together, about what we can use these extraordinary technologies to do.

title: Fifa president Infantino will stand for re-election
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino will stand for re-election in March, the world governing body has confirmed.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino will stand for re-election in March, says football's world governing body.

Infantino, who has filled the role since 2016, has been under pressure following his scrapped plan to sell stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment firms.

Infantino's lucrative plan sparked a global outcry, with European football's governing body Uefa threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.

"The Fifa president announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027," read a Fifa statement.

"Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election."

Infantino refused to answer questions about his future when asked by reporters at the Women's Under-20 World Cup in Poland on Saturday.

It is the first time Fifa has said he will run for a new term since the plan was announced following the summer's World Cup.

Should the 56-year-old Swiss be re-elected, he will serve until 2031.

Fifa this week accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership", in a challenge to litigation over Infantino's plan.

Last week Uefa filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.

Division, drama and power - what next for Infantino and Uefa?

As recently as mid-July Infantino was considered a certainty to be re-elected.

All but a handful of Fifa members had endorsed him, and he faced no meaningful challenge.

However, the Football Associations of England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland are among those to have publicly withdrawn support since Infantino's plan was announced.

BBC Sport understands Uefa is confident that a candidate can be found to stand against Infantino.

A candidate must receive the backing of at least 106 of the 211 Fifa member associations.

Uefa has abandoned the idea of trying to force a vote of no confidence.

It would require three-quarters of the members - 159 votes - to pass the motion through a change of Fifa statutes, which is considered unrealistic.

No candidates to challenge Infantino have been named, although Concacaf president Victor Montagliani is considered a serious option.

Nominations must be submitted by 18 November.

fullText:
NEW YORK — It's probably fitting that in the world's economic and marketing capital, a Grand Slam tennis tournament doubles as one giant product-placement opportunity.

Little-known players who play on stadium courts end up with last-minute patches stuck onto their kits. Their lesser-known coaches wear hats from brands such as the IT company Infosys and the used-car retailer Carvana.

The week before the U.S. Open is a strange mélange of tennis-related activations. Aryna Sabalenka appears at a Brooklyn Heights pizza joint to promote an energy drink. The Waldorf Astoria puts a tennis court in its famed ballroom for an exhibition with Tommy Paul, Maria Sakkari, Ben Shelton and Leylah Fernandez to promote its new global racquet club venture. Jannik Sinner, injured and back home, chimes in from afar on social media, saying he misses everyone at the U.S. Open, including "@baccarathotels and the whole team who always makes me feel at home."

As the field gets winnowed down and all but the biggest stars and some supporting characters remain, there's a pretty good chance tennis fans might scratch their heads and wonder why so many coaches are wearing swag with one of two or three ubiquitous logos.

One of the most prominent is Eight Sleep.

The company makes high-tech mattress covers that users can heat or cool to their desired temperature. The product tracks sleep patterns and measures users' quality of rest. It is not to be confused with IM8, the nutritional supplement company co-founded by David Beckham.

IM8 has Sabalenka as an ambassador. Her coaching staff has worn IM8 swag, though things can get confusing because her coach, Anton Dubrov, is now part of the Eight Sleep team.

Sabalenka, the two-time reigning champion and world No. 1, plays most of her matches in Arthur Ashe Stadium and many of those in primetime. The camera often shifts to her coaching box. That's a lot of airtime for Eight Sleep, even though Sabalenka does not directly endorse the company.

Dubrov does. So does Frédéric Fontang, who coaches Jiří Lehečka, and Michael Russell, who coaches Taylor Fritz, and Jamie Delgado, who coaches Grigor Dimitrov.

On Russell, the logo for Eight Sleep has to fight for attention, since Russell is the closest thing tennis coaching has to a NASCAR driver. He wears patches from Waterdrop and Solinco. Hats from Eight Sleep and Papatui, a men's skincare brand founded by Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson. Sometimes, Russell wears a Carvana shirt.

Carvana is another of the logos that are everywhere at this U.S. Open — it's on the coaching teams of Amanda Anisimova, Madison Keys and many more.

Alexandra Zatarain, a co-founder of Eight Sleep, said the company has worked with athletes, including Fritz, but these days it often makes more sense to work with their coaches.

They are the ones who set a player's routine, working with a nutritionist on what they eat, and with a physiotherapist and fitness trainer to plan the athlete's preparation and recovery, practices that have become far more complex over the last decade. Optimizing sleep is a big part of that.

"We had this idea of just, 'Oh, what if we make the coaches our partners because they are actually a really important partner in making sure that the player stays on track in terms of all of their health,'" Zatarain said.

And, fortuitously for would-be sponsors, something happened in tennis that made these arrangements even more appealing. Coaches are allowed to coach more openly. They don't have to speak with hidden signals, like removing a hat when they want a player to serve wide or standing and clapping when they want the player to move closer to the net.

In 2022, the U.S. Open launched a trial that allowed off-court coaching during matches for the first time. The other Grand Slams followed the next year. In 2025, World Tennis, the sport's world governing body, changed the rules, allowing it essentially everywhere.

The interplay between players and their coaches often generates some of the most dramatic viewing moments of a tennis match. So, the camera finds them — a lot.

"The coaches, I think, are getting a little bit more visibility," Zatarain said.

Their jobs have also changed in recent years, as teams have grown and coaching a top player has become a sophisticated operation. In the best and most serious environments, it's something like being a chief operating officer of a Formula 1 team, where the player is the car.

Enter the relationships with companies that seek to improve the health of people who may or may not compete in sports. There are only so many tennis players who care about what kind of strings a coach and player might prefer. But everybody sleeps. And a lot of people take energy supplements, including just about every player on tour.

"It's like a holistic approach," Fontang said,  "with clear goals, a clear process and to something that you do consistently right as well in the process. This is how you bring consistency into the match."

Fontang played on the tour in the 1990s, which is now considered a prehistoric era in terms of recovery science. He did a little stretching and mobility work before and after he played. Occasionally, he might get attention from a tour trainer or physiotherapist. He certainly didn't have one on his team.

Ivan Lendl, a star of the 1980s, was the first major men's player known to focus on health and wellness. Martina Navratilova was the first woman.

They both won a lot. Other players noticed.

Now, everything is tracked. Blood gets tested to monitor training and recovery. Nearly everyone rides a stationary bike — high tension, low speed — after a match and quickly downs a protein recovery drink.

And therein lies the opportunity. What separates the Eight Sleeps and IM8s and Solincos of the world is that they have an actual use in the sport, compared with a random resort company that just uses a coach as a billboard. A couple of years ago, Fritz had Eight Sleep install a mattress pad in his hotel room in New York.

Nearly every player goes through a sophisticated recovery routine, but the common denominator is the most valuable recovery activity of all.

"Sleep is the first thing that is the most important," Dubrov said after a late match — a common occurrence at the U.S. Open. Everything else will get cut short so that Sabalenka can maximize the amount of time she can spend in bed, though quality can count as much as quantity.

The hot European summer was not great. There isn't much air conditioning in London homes.

"You can have like 10 hours of the sleep," Dubrov said. "But you're going to be kind of awake for most of it."

Russell said he was introduced to Eight Sleep by Fritz, who has long had sleep issues because he can spend a lot of time playing video games. As a teenager, he got in trouble with USTA coaches because he was often gaming until 4 a.m. It's healthier than clubbing, but still not great.

His team noticed improvements in his sleep data in recent years. Maybe it's his mattress pad. Maybe it's a placebo effect, which Russell calls "the most powerful drug there is."

And a clear branding opportunity, present even as Fritz lost Saturday in five sets to Argentina's Francisco Cerúndolo.

So, no matter who advances to the second week of this marquee tournament, expect plenty more sponsorship and caps that look like they could be plentiful at company retreats.

title: Katie Taylor bows out as three-time undisputed champion
description: Katie Taylor brought her remarkable boxing career to a close in front of 80,000 jubilant fans at Croke Park, bowing out as a three-time undisputed world champion.The Bray native produced a dominant pe...
fullText:
Katie Taylor brought her remarkable boxing career to a close in front of 80,000 jubilant fans at Croke Park, bowing out as a three-time undisputed world champion.

The Bray native produced a dominant performance against unbeaten Flora Pili, securing a points victory to claim the vacant WBC light-welterweight title and complete an extraordinary final chapter.

Taylor finishes her career with 26 victories from 27 professional contests, having established herself as one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures.

The 40-year-old's farewell in Dublin was a night of celebration, spectacle and music, with Croke Park providing a fitting stage for the final appearance of a fighter who has transformed women's boxing.

And among the many supporters celebrating Taylor's achievements were Leeds United fans, with the former Republic of Ireland footballer having long spoken about her affection for the Whites.

Appearing on Soccer AM in 2019, Taylor revealed the origins of her Leeds connection.

"My team is actually Leeds United.

"My dad is from Leeds and my older two brothers grew up supporting Leeds as well. Every Christmas we would get Leeds jerseys for Christmas and football boots. I was a huge football fan growing up."

Taylor has previously described her visits to Elland Road as "some of my best memories as a kid", while her love of the club has remained throughout her hugely successful boxing career.

That connection was strengthened in 2021 when Taylor brought her world championship belts to Leeds, successfully defending her titles against Jennifer Han at Headingley Stadium.

Now, five years on from her night in Leeds, Taylor has called time on a career which saw her become a three-time undisputed world champion and one of the most influential figures in the history of women's sport.

Her final victory over Pili ensured she departed the sport on her own terms, adding another world title to a glittering collection before receiving the farewell she deserved in front of 80,000 fans at Croke Park.

From the football pitches of Ireland to the biggest stages in boxing, Taylor's journey has been extraordinary.

And for Leeds United supporters, she will always be remembered as one of their own.

title: Bill Madden: Tampa Bay Rays ready to usher in new era with stadium relocation near
description: NEW YORK — For years baseball people have marveled at the Tampa Bay Rays’ ability to remain competitive in the American League East despite consistently low industry payrolls and annual attendance. fullText:
NEW YORK — For years baseball people have marveled at the Tampa Bay Rays' ability to remain competitive in the American League East despite consistently low industry payrolls and annual attendance. Since 2008, the Rays have been to the postseason nine times, including the World Series twice, always with payrolls of well over $100 million less than the Yankees.

At the same time, Tampa Bay fans have gotten used to the Rays' jettisoning their favorite players (See: Isaac Paredes, Randy Arozarena, Brandon Lowe and Tyler Glasnow in just the last three years) as soon as they became too costly or near free agency. And with the clock continuing to tick on their expiring (2028) lease at dreary Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Fla., there's never been a sense of permanence of the Rays in Tampa Bay.

Recently, both the Tampa city council and the Hillsborough County commissioners voted to approve a new $2.3 billion mixed-use stadium project near Hillsborough College's Dale Mabry Boulevard campus, not far from Raymond James Stadium, the home of the NFL Tampa Bay Bucs. The plan is similar to what the Atlanta Braves constructed in Cobb County, Ga., in 2015 for a stadium surrounded by a village of shops and restaurants that would produce addition revenue for the team.

It was always the accepted view of most folks in the Tampa Bay area that if the Rays were going to survive they would have to be in Tampa where the large majority of their 3 1/2 million residents are. This was part of the reason the Rays have remained one of the top revenue sharing recipients in baseball, an average of nearly $60 million a year. That's on top of the $50 million they and the other 29 clubs receive annually from the MLB Central Fund. So they've had the money to increase payroll, but the previous Rays owner Stu Sternberg just chose not to spend it.

If the owners are able to establish a cap in the new collective bargaining agreement, revenue sharing would go away, but the Rays are anticipating revenues of far more than $60 million from the new park and surrounding village which is now slated to be ready by 2029. For sure, now that the stadium issue has finally been resolved, the Rays, under their new ownership led by Jacksonville developer Patrick Zalupski, are expected to be operating vastly different. Last week Zalupski told the Tampa Bay Times: "Tampa's the No. 11 media market in the country. There's nothing holding it back, "adding that with the new ballpark and the development around it, "we should be able to drive payroll (currently 27th at $116,208,358) into the top 15 circle and maybe even the top 10."

In the meantime, the Rays have been leading the American League East since June 27, but will be facing their biggest challenge now in the September stretch, starting with this present road trip through Texas where they snapped a 10-game skid at Globe Life Field as of Friday, and three in Atlanta against the Braves. They then finish the season with three games with the Red Sox, four in New York with the Yankees and three more at home with the Phillies.

That four-game series at Yankee Stadium Sept. 22-24 figures to be the biggest regular-season series for both the Rays and the Yankees in years, especially since the Yankees expect to be (Aaron Judge) whole, while Rays GM Eric Neander made significant upgrades to his pitching at the trade deadline with Freddy Peralta from the Mets and hard-throwing righty reliever Tyler Wells from the Orioles, and in perhaps the best acquisition of all, filled the Rays longstanding need — a catcher who can hit — by landing Liam Hicks from the Marlins

If the Rays are able to emerge through that gauntlet still atop the AL East it should be cause for considerable concern for the Yankees. Because as improved as they've become this year, they figure to be this good and better for years to come with one of the top player development systems in baseball with a half dozen top 100 prospects including outfielders Theo Gillen, Jake Melton and Austin Overn and catcher Caden Bodine, all of whom could be making their debuts at some point next year.

In every way, the baseball future couldn't be brighter in Tampa Bay.

title: Three reasons Wisconsin shocks the world vs. Notre Dame in Week 1
description: The Wisconsin Badgers are finally looking to kickstart things under head coach Luke Fickell, who enters his fourth full season with the program.
fullText:
The Wisconsin Badgers are finally looking to kickstart things under head coach Luke Fickell, who will soon be entering his fourth full season with the program.

While things aren't completely dire, if the Badgers show another year of regression under the former Cincinnati coach, then his reign may come to an end.

However, all of that can change with a strong 2026 season. Overall, the Badgers have a workable schedule that sees them missing out on playing against Oregon, Michigan, Ohio State, or Indiana. All they have to do is start things right against the Notre Dame Fighting Irish, who come into the season ranked No. 4 in the AP Poll and No. 5 in the US LBM Coaches Poll.

Today's task is to look at the three reasons why this upset is on the cards

The Irish struggle to close out games prior to October, with their only two losses last season occurring before September 14, and who could forget their shock loss to the Northern Illinois Huskies the season prior. It's not quite known why the first few weeks of the season generate a slow start, but it is clear that if there is a time to face them, it's sooner rather than later.

It has been a long time since a Wisconsin backfield has looked as promising as it does with Sama and Joseph. During his time in the Big 12, Sama compiled four games where he rushed for over 100 yards. Joseph leaves Old Dominion with nine games of at least 250 passing yards and four games of at least 100 rushing yards in his career, so it's clear these two can single-handedly take games by the scruff of the neck if the Irish aren't careful.

It is easy to remember all of the faults last year's offense compiled, but it is harder to remember that despite facing seven teams ranked inside the AP Top 25, the Badgers only allowed 323.6 yards per game, good enough for 23rd-best in the country. With transfers like safety Marvin Burks Jr. and the Irish's ability to start off slow, the Badgers' defense could find ways to break the game open.

title: Changing the world one vegetable at a time: UK first carbon-negative greengrocer
description: I spent a day with the UK's first carbon-negative greengrocers who are changing the future for generations to come, right here in Leicester
fullText:
This story was published by the Leicester Gazette: a local, independent newspaper about Leicestershire. 1,000 people have already joined our mailing list. Just use that button below to 

No spam. Unsubscribe anytime. Want to support our work? Click here for membership.

Leicester is associated with many great things: its cultural quarter, the space industry, and its dynamic culinary scene, to name a few. But in the city there’s innovation happening quietly, one delivery at a time. I recently learned that Leicester is home to the UK's first carbon-negative mobile greengrocers. I was in the middle of renovating my Clarendon Park flat – and was caked in sawdust – when I saw it: a brilliantly decorated 1950s milk float, with fruit and vegetables instead of milk, and the words ‘slow-moving veg’ written on the back.

Naturally, in a disheveled state, I walked up to the driver, told him I was a reporter, and expressed my interest in writing about them. I got a business card in return. In the weeks that followed, my editor green-lit a feature on the greengrocer, and I set a date for an interview. What followed was probably one of the most pleasant Friday mornings I’ve had in a long time, as I joined the Green Tomato team on one of their routes around Stoneygate.

I arrive at the home of the Green Tomato founders, husband and wife team Nisha and Manoj. One of their employees, Callum, is there – he’s back from a 4am trip to Leicester's wholesale market, and has helped load the float, which is parked outside on the driveway.

Before we even set off, the community feel which the Green Tomato is built around is evident: “hey mate,” shouts a postman as he power-walks across the road. He hands Manoj a couple of letters and the two chat briefly about the weather. Then, as he turns to leave, Manoj hands him an apple from the float. “It’s his favourite apple,” Nisha later tells me when I ask her about it.

So we hit the road, and less than five minutes later we’ve arrived at our first stop in Stoneygate, and the first customer opens their front door, reusable carrier bags in hand. I learn that his name is Stuart.

Once Stuart has finished his shopping, I ask him: “How long have you shopped with the Green Tomato?”

“Since Covid days, wasn’t it?” He asks Manoj – who nods in response, “Six years now, it’s going to be six years in July.

“And I’m still only 53,” he says, which is met with chuckles from Manoj and Nisha.

I ask him about Leicester Market as well, and why he doesn't shop there. “I don’t go into central Leicester, I’m retired,” he responds. “I visit Boots to have my eyes and ears tested, and that’s about the only time I go in.”

But anyway, “this is a great local business”, he says. And with that, Stuart heads back into his house, carrier bags of produce in hand.

The float departs, and snakes its way through the streets of Stoneygate, stopping to make deliveries as we go. As Manoj fills his customers’ bags with fresh produce, they chat away about all sorts. He's well aware of what's going on in his customers’ lives, and they discuss topics ranging from customers' families to holidays (Manoj and Nisha are going to Türkiye and will be missed dearly by their customers) and, in keeping with the older demographic of the customers on this particular route, various age-related medical topics. The relationship between the Green Tomato and its customer base is a close one, and the conversations are reminiscent of catchup between friends rather than a vendor and a buyer.

On this particular route, most of the customers are retirees, Nisha tells me. But the Green Tomatoes' other routes through Clarendon Park and Knighton attract customers of all ages.

We pull up outside the front door of another regular. “Manoj is a treasure – write that down,” he tells me, after he’s finished shopping. He’s a retired professor with a characterful received accent. “He is the best thing that’s ever happened to me; there’s lots of people – like me – who can’t get out to get fresh fruit and veg.” The Green Tomato is “absolutely marvellous,” as far as he is concerned.

Convenience is the main draw for customers in Stoneygate, “it’s somebody coming to your door, and it’s a personal service,” says one. “It’s the human touch – that’s the most important thing,” says another.

After the route had ended, Nisha and I spent around 20 minutes chatting about the Green Tomato.

“We have family in India and every time we visit, the best part of our visit is where the stall comes,” she says. “It’s pulled by a person normally, and it's got fresh produce from local farms.  There’s no packaging.”

She continues, “nobody in India goes to do their fresh food shop in a supermarket. It's not a thing. Nobody does that.

“It's frustrating that people are not doing more; there's so much evidence now of human activity and the impact on our environment, and yet behaviour change is difficult. I thought this would actually kill two birds with one stone. By bringing the shop to the doorstep, we're going to be zero emissions.”

The Green Tomato has three separate routes: one in Knighton, one in Clarendon Park, and one in Stoneygate. Something to note is that these are nice areas of Leicester, known for being desirable places to live which are pretty well-off (the Guardian wrote 14 years ago of ‘corduroyed lecturers in cafés’ and ‘legendary cheeseboards’ in Clarendon Park and that certainly still rings true today).

This is something I wanted to ask about, but I'm beaten to the punch when Nisha says, “Our suppliers are brilliant, but the cost of our buying is more than the supermarket prices. So, although we want the business to be accessible to everyone, in fact, it's just not turned out like that.”

At the end of the day, the Green Tomato is a business, and “We need to remain profitable to do all the things that we do,” says Nisha. “We've ended up with a very niche customer base, which we're fully aware of. But we want to open up to everyone, and that will involve help.”

What that help looks like isn’t yet clear to the Tomato, but Nisha assures me that expanding the business and reaching more customers is high up on their agenda. Some support may come from councils or from charities. “One of the targets for local councils is to be able to provide fresh fruit and veg in certain areas where it's difficult,” says Nisha. It’s early days yet, and while talks are happening and Nisha has “made a few inroads,” there’s not yet a solid plan in place that she’s ready to share with me.

One thing I’m struck by is the sense of community the Green Tomato has managed to build. I’ve reported previously on Leicester Market, and have had traders speak to me extensively about the value of community. It seems it doesn't matter if you're on a stall or on the streets, that community is fuelling independent small businesses throughout the city.

Before you go… We’ve recently surpassed 1,000 subscribers, which is amazing considering we’re a small team on a shoestring budget.

Now, we’re ready for the next stage of the Leicester Gazette. Download our new app and get all of our journalism anytime, anywhere.

The app connects with Bluesky, Mastodon and Threads, giving you access to a network of around 60 million people. It’s a safer, more meaningful alternative to mainstream social media – owned by the community.

title: Wrexham boss Parkinson says Swansea captain should have seen red
description: The Wrexham boss claimed the Wales international's challenge on Callum O'Hare was a 'leg-breaker'
fullText:
Wrexham manager Phil Parkinson says Swansea City captain Ben Cabango got away with a "leg-breaking challenge" in their Welsh derby stalemate.

Parkinson claimed the Wales defender should have been given a straight red for the lunge on midfielder Callum O'Hare late on in the match at the Swansea.com Stadium.

Cabango, who had come on as a second-half substitute, was booked for the foul that prompted an angry reaction from the visitors' bench.

O'Hare was replaced soon after as Swansea maintained their unbeaten start to the season to stay top of the early Championship table.

"I know we want to protect our players but, when someone flies in at that speed, that could have been a leg-breaking challenge," Parkinson said.

"I thought the referee handled the atmosphere well, but in the big decision he didn't make the right call.

"I don't think anybody in the ground or whether people watching back on TV can deny that."

Swansea stay unbeaten but are frustrated by Wrexham in Welsh derby

Eyes on big prize as Swansea and Wrexham collide

More to come from Swansea, insists Matos

Cabango missed the ball in the 77th minute challenge and caught O'Hare, who was making his debut after a £6.5m deadline day move from Sheffield United.

Swansea boss Vitor Matos did not want to get involved in the debate after the game, saying: "I never comment on ref decisions, in one way or the other. If he [Parkinson] says that, good for him."

O'Hare claimed Cabango should have been sent off, saying the 16-cap centre-back told him he "didn't touch" the midfielder.

Parkinson added: "Cabango grabbed Kieffer around the neck on the halfway line before that. A yellow card and then the tackle.

"But I'm very interested to ask the referee when he compares both those incidents. How he differentiates between the two, because every year, managers have to sit and listen to the referees about what they deem to be red cards, and when you're out of control, like Ben Cabango was and endangering a player. Wrexham still had chances to win the game, but Parkinson said he was pleased with the efforts of his side on the back of a first win of the season, Wednesday's midweek triumph at Millwall.

title: Taylor crowns career in stylish Croke Park triumph
description: Katie Taylor ends illustrious career as a three-time undisputed world champion as Croke Park gave one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures the grandest of farewells.
fullText:
Katie Taylor ended her illustrious career as a three-time undisputed world champion as Croke Park gave one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures the grandest of farewells on a night of celebration, spectacle and music.

The 40-year-old outclassed unbeaten Flora Pili on points in front of 80,000 jubilant fans to add the vacant WBC belt to her WBA, WBO and IBF light-welterweight titles.

With the footwork, speed and sharp pressure fighting that defined her career, Taylor produced one final stylish performance against the overmatched Frenchwoman to win by scores of 100-90, 100-90 and 98-91.

Promoter Eddie Hearn paid tribute to Taylor, calling her "Ireland's greatest sportsperson", before she took one final lap of the ring, waving to the crowd before ceremonially placing her gloves and belts in the centre of the canvas.

After almost a quarter of a century in the sport, Taylor - an Olympic champion, two-weight world champion and one of the pioneers of women's professional boxing - finally got her fairytale ending at her dream venue.

She bows out with a record of 26 wins and just one defeat, but this was about more than one final result.

It was a night steeped in Irish pride, with a spine-tingling atmosphere and chart-topping pop group Westlife helping provide a fitting send-off.

Taylor signs off career in style with unanimous decision win against Pili - reaction

Tears, blood & triumph - Taylor's iconic career in pictures

On an unforgettable night for the city, around 80 per cent of those inside Croke Park had never previously attended a boxing event, but turned out to honour a fighter who dragged women's sport from the margins and took an entire nation on her journey.

The crowd was the sixth largest recorded post-war attendance for a boxing event anywhere in the world. By early evening, the stands were awash with green and white, tricolours draped over shoulders.

Westlife performed 'World of Our Own' and 'You Raise Me Up', with tens of thousands joining in as phone lights flickered around the towering tiers of Croke Park.

The atmosphere softened for an a cappella version of 'Grace', the well-known Irish ballad linked to the 1916 Easter Rising, before the national anthem rang out.

Chants of "Ole, Ole, Ole" drowned out Pili's ringwalk music before Taylor finally emerged to 'All Hail King Jesus', a nod to the faith she has spoken so openly about throughout her career.

She stretched her arms wide, sang along and tried to take in every second of her final walk to the ring. There was emotion on her face, but also the familiar focus as fireworks shot into the Dublin sky.

Taylor had spent fight week insisting there was still a job to do, but even for a fighter who had sold out Madison Square Garden and performed on some of boxing's grandest stages, it was hard to imagine her being untouched by a reception like this.

'One of the best' - boxing world reacts to Taylor's farewell win

After a quiet opener, Taylor - who turned professional in 2016 - burst into life in the second round, firing quick combinations before darting back out of range.

She repeatedly beat Pili to the punch, working in bursts and making the most of the two-minute rounds.

Pili, 29, arrived unbeaten in 12 contests and had previously held the European title. With little expectation on her shoulders, she had everything to gain.

But she had never faced anyone remotely close to Taylor's level and the gulf in class soon began to show.

The party atmosphere continued between rounds as it became increasingly clear there would be no gatecrashing from the Frenchwoman.

Former world champion Prince Naseem Hamed and UFC star Paddy Pimblett watched from ringside as Pili swung wildly in the fifth, only for Taylor to make her miss and fire back.

Pili enjoyed her best spell in the seventh, a quick flurry briefly snapping Taylor's head back, but it did little to alter the direction of the fight.

Croke Park rose for the final two minutes as Taylor continued to press forward, letting her hands go while the noise poured down from the stands.

She embraced her mother, trainer and manager in the ring as 'Celebration' rang around Croke Park before the inevitable result was read out.

"Let me just look around for a second", she said afterwards, soaking up every ounce of the reception.

Taylor has been unequivocal that Croke Park would be the end and she walks away having beaten every opponent she faced as a professional.

Her only defeat came against Chantelle Cameron in Dublin in 2023. Six months later, Taylor returned to the 3Arena and avenged it to become undisputed champion in a second weight division.

After the final bell, she paid tribute to her family and somehow held the tears back as she spoke to the crowd.

"There's nothing like an Irish mammy," she said, smiling as she thanked those closest to her.

For a fighter who has never hidden her dislike of media interviews, there was something striking about the confidence with which she walked around the ring, microphone in hand, soaking up the final moments.

"We did it. We brought boxing back to Croke Park. You were with me in London 2012, you were with me with the heartbreak of Rio. You stayed with me when I turned pro," Taylor said.

"I don't know any other country that would sell 80,000 tickets for a female athlete. I'm convinced Ireland is the only country."

Taylor will forever be defined by her trilogy wins against Amanda Serrano and leaves with a staggering list of accolades, but her true impact cannot be measured in statistics alone.

That legacy belongs to the young girl who once pretended to be a boy just to box when girls were not allowed.

She fought tirelessly to get the sport sanctioned in Ireland and included in the Olympics, before going on to conquer both the amateur and professional codes.

The belts will eventually gather dust, but the trail Taylor blazed across the sport will never fade.

title: 'One of the best' - boxing world reacts to Taylor's farewell win
description: Some of the biggest names in women's boxing pay tribute to Katie Taylor after the Irish great ended her career with victory over Flora Pili at Croke Park.
fullText:
Some of the biggest names in women's boxing have paid tribute to Katie Taylor after the Irish great ended her career with victory over Flora Pili at Croke Park.

Unified lightweight champion Caroline Dubois called Taylor "one of the best to ever do it", while Claressa Shields said the 40-year-old deserved to "ride off into the sunset".

Taylor beat Pili on points in Dublin to become undisputed light-welterweight champion and retires with 26 wins from 27 professional contests, Olympic gold and three undisputed title triumphs across two divisions.

"Thank you so much for paving the way," Londoner Dubois wrote on X. "Wishing you happiness, success and joy for this next season."

Taylor was sharper throughout, repeatedly beating the Frenchwoman to the punch before finishing with one final burst of combinations as the crowd rose to its feet.

American Shields - the self-proclaimed Greatest Woman of All Time - added: "Congrats Katie. Now ride off into the sunset. You deserve it all."

Super-featherweight champion Alycia Baumgardner described Taylor as "a trailblazer who helped set the stage for all of us".

"What a legacy," she wrote. "It's been a privilege watching your journey from the beginning."

Taylor's farewell unfolded in front of more than 80,000 fans in Dublin, with Westlife performing before the main event and Croke Park providing a fitting backdrop to her final night.

Former world champion Carl Frampton said Taylor's relationship with the Irish public was unlike anything else in boxing.

"You can tell that she doesn't enjoy doing stuff in front of the media, but she still has this adulation from everybody," the Northern Irishman said.

"Katie Taylor is different, she's special and there will never be another one like her."

Former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew described the occasion as one of the most remarkable exits the sport had seen.

"I don't think in all of my years of watching this game, I have seen an exit as beautiful, amazing and fitting," he said.

"She has just retired as the greatest champion ever. I have never seen a fighter leave as an undisputed champion on their own terms."

Former world champion Barry Jones picked out the final 20 seconds, when Taylor produced the kind of rapid combinations which defined so many of her biggest fights.

"That's what you really remember about her," he said on the Dazn broadcast.

"Those rallies of big punches, combinations and that's how she finished her last fight."

American Mikaela Mayer - who was also ringside - was struck by the final image of Taylor placing her gloves in the centre of the ring.

"I was sitting there watching her put her gloves in the centre of the ring and it's like a story," she said.

Taylor had long dreamed of fighting at Croke Park and had made clear she wanted the stadium to stage the final chapter of her career.

Bellew said there was "no way" Taylor would return to boxing, although he could see her remaining involved by mentoring younger fighters.

"She will always be there to give her advice, speak to her and help her," he said.

"But ultimately she will sail off into the sunset and who could possibly deserve it more."

title: UN votes to adopt new map that makes our world look different
description: The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to adopt a new world map that reflects countries’ true relative sizes, after African nations urged the UN to right a centuries-old wrong.
fullText:
The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to adopt a new world map that reflects countries’ true relative sizes, after African nations urged the UN to right a centuries-old wrong.

The “Correct the Map” resolution –– put forward by African Union member states, as well as the Bahamas –– passed with overwhelming support: 164 member states voted in favor, six abstained and only the United States voted against it.

The resolution aims to give an “equitable” representation of the globe’s regions, particularly Africa, arguing that the distortions in the current world map mean the continent has undergone a “symbolic minimization” in people’s collective imagination.

At present, many of the world’s maps are based on the Mercator projection, created by European cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569. It is widely used for navigation since the north-south lines have constant true bearings relative to the equator.

However, it is less useful as a world map since the scale is distorted, with countries further from the equator appearing disproportionately larger than those closest. For example, on the Mercator, Greenland appears larger than the continent of South America and appears similar in size to Africa.

In reality, Greenland is roughly the size of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Africa is 14 times the size of Greenland.

Some critics of the Mercator projection suspect it has remained widely used because it enlarges and centers Europe, as well as other Western regions such as North America, perpetuating ideas of European superiority.

The UN resolution notes “with concern that this distortion contributes to minimizing the perceived sizes of Africa, Latin America and South Asia, and perpetuating an unbalanced view of the world.”

It adds that the distortions also “contribute to minimizing the extent of socioeconomic realities, infrastructure needs, development potential and prosperity in the Southern regions, and that they can fuel prejudices in the environmental, geopolitical and security fields.”

The resolution therefore proposes, as an “act of cognitive justice and memorial reparation,” that the Mercator projection is replaced with the Equal Earth projection, which depicts the relative surface areas of the world’s regions more accurately.

In the Equal Earth, which was introduced at the 2018 North American Cartographic Information Society conference, Europe appears to shrink, Brazil balloons, and Greenland dramatically diminishes. Africa appears much larger in comparison.

France’s foreign affairs minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, announced Friday that France “will abandon the Mercator projection” in favor of representations that more accurately depict countries’ surface areas, state-owned TV network France 24 reported.

“The United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia,” Barrot said, adding that “distortions eventually take root in perceptions” and that “the time has come to correct them.”

The UN vote comes after the African Union adopted the Equal Earth Map in March and after Togo, on behalf of the AU, asked UN member states in April to do the same. As a result, a draft resolution was created and the UN General Assembly held informal consultations on it in July.

“Africa, once diminished on maps, now insists on being seen at its true scale – geographically, historically, morally, culturally, economically, diplomatically and globally,” Amma Twum-Amoah, commissioner for the AU’s Department of Health, Humanitarian Affairs and Social Development, said in a statement in March.

New Zealand has also taken issue with the Mercator map, with a tourism ad back in 2018 – featuring then-Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern – joking that “New Zealand is disappearing off the world maps” due to its position in the bottom right-hand corner.

The Equal Earth map addresses this, coming in various forms, including one that centers Oceania, rather than Greenwich, London. Greenwich has long been used as the standard for world time and global geographical reference.

Digital map platforms such as Google Maps also currently use a version of the Mercator projection. The draft resolution urges tech platforms to engage with UN member states and regional organizations and adopt the more accurate projection.

title: South Africa finish strongly to take 2-1 series lead against All Blacks
description: South Africa eventually overpower a spirited New Zealand as the world champions came on strong in the final quarter in Soweto to take a 2-1 series lead.
fullText:
Greatest Rivalry Series - third Test

Tries: Arendse, penalty try, Kriel, Marx Cons: Mngomezulu 2 Pens: Mngomezulu

Tries: Savea 2, Jordan, Taukei'aho Cons: Love, McKenzie

South Africa eventually overpowered a spirited New Zealand, who could only outrun their hosts' set-piece power for so long, as the world champions came on strong in the final quarter in Soweto to take a 2-1 lead in a high-quality 'Greatest Rivalry' series.

The two sides traded two tries each in a tight first half, with New Zealand's composure and ambition with ball in hand stretching South Africa's onrushing defence.

The All Blacks sniffed a famous victory when Will Jordan chased after his own kick ahead and crossed for a 17-12 lead in the 55th minute.

But, shortly after, Jesse Kriel barged through Leroy Carter to cross at the other end and, reprieved, South Africa took full advantage.

Malcolm Marx plunged over at the back of juggernaut maul and a Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu penalty gave South Africa a cushion that Samisoni Taukei'aho's final-play try could dent, but not fully deflate.

The two teams will meet in a fourth and final Test in the American city of Baltimore next weekend, with New Zealand, who won the opening match, looking to snatch a draw in the series.

With Springbok captain Siya Kolisi calling on his team to honour those who died in nearby Soweto during the fight against apartheid, and national pride stung by New Zealand coach Dave Rennie's criticism of their scrum technique, Soccer City was braced for a fast start by the hosts.

New Zealand's smarts initially defused the fire and fury inside the cauldron, however.

After a brave Peter Lakai turnover had halted South Africa momentum, Will Jordan streaked clear to switch play to the other 22.

South Africa fly-half Feinberg-Mngomezulu was shown yellow for knocking down Ardie Savea's offload and, from the resulting penalty, the All Blacks rolled round the back of a short-range line-out, clearing room for Savea to sweep through some under-staffed fringe defence and score.

With Cheslin Kolbe, with a perfect goal-kicking record so far in the series, having departed with a head knock, South Africa had taken a dent to their confidence, as well as the scoreboard.

New Zealand had ducked and dived to minimise the effect of South Africa's set-piece supremacy.

Fast strikes from hooker Asafo Aumua had got the ball away from a fast-retreating scrum, while trick plays and the addition of Lakai as a jumping option kept South Africa from competing successfully at the line-out.

South Africa built momentum regardless though and All Black discipline frayed as Damian de Allende shrugged off Carter and fed Kurt-Lee Arendse to score in the 21st minute after a string of penalty offences from the away side.

New Zealand pulled back 12-5 ahead soon after with the agility and speed of second rows Sam Darry and Tupou Vaa'i buying territory and Savea on hand to scoop up and scoot over following Arendse's tackle on Carter out wide.

It is impossible to keep the South Africa's coshing scrum power out of the game, however.

Rennie had accused South Africa's front row of 'walking around' their opposite numbers in their second Test win in Cape Town last weekend. Marx, Wilco Louw and Ox Nche duly took route one, ploughing through the All Blacks front row to force a penalty try and ensure parity at half-time.

While another Test awaits in the United States, the sense of an unofficial series being on the line was tangible.

New Zealand have won on South African soil only once before, when the Incomparables of 1996 returned with a 2-1 victory.

Fly-half Ruben Love missed a long-range shot at goal after the interval with the stakes suffocatingly high.

Jordan's try, from Carter's pop off the floor, briefly opened up scoreboard space on 55 minutes, but South Africa edged ahead for the first time two minutes later as Kriel shrugged off a soft tackle and scampered in.

The hosts took a 19-17 advantage into the final quarter and, with the All Blacks lacking Savea's leadership after their captain was forced off with a shoulder injury in the first half, the Boks landed a knockout blow in familiar fashion.

Scrum pressure forced New Zealand replacement Fletcher Newell to his knees, the Springboks punted the resulting penalty into the 22m and a monster maul rumbled infield and forward with Marx crashing over.

Feinberg-Mngomezulu added the extras for a 26-17 lead and slotted a 70th-minute penalty to push the lead out to 12 points.

The 85,976-strong crowd went through their celebratory songbook, dusting off their Cranberries-inspired ode to head coach Rassie Erasmus.

Taukei'aho's try was too little, too late to change the tune of the contest, but the rest of the rugby world will take heart from how hard his side have pushed the Springboks in all three of their meetings.

title: Modric plans to play for Croatia past 41st birthday
description: Luke Modric, 41, is not ready to retire from international football and hopes to play for Croatia in upcoming Nations League games, including against England.
fullText:
Luka Modric turns 41 on Wednesday but is not ready to retire from international football just yet.

The Croatia FA has announced, external that their captain intends to continue playing for the national team in upcoming Nations League games, including against England.

His decision coincides with the return of Slaven Bilic as manager, with the former West Ham boss helping to guide Modric's fledgling international career in his first stint in charge of the Croatia side, between 2006 and 2012.

Modric earned his first senior cap in March 2006, just before Bilic was named Croatia manager for the first time, and has since gone on to make 202 appearances for his country.

He was expected to call it a day after this summer's World Cup, when Zlatko Dalic's side were knocked out in the last 32 by Portugal.

"Of course, Luka's decision makes me extremely happy," said Bilic, who was manager of Croatia when they denied Steve McLaren's England side qualification for the 2008 Euros.

"We are all aware what he brings to Croatia, both on and off the pitch.

"I'm looking forward to working with him again, after 14 years, and we both share a strong ambition to keep Croatia a top, successful team, shoulder to shoulder with the best teams in the world."

Modric, who currently plays for AC Milan, won the Golden Ball at the 2018 World Cup in Russia, when he helped Croatia reach the final, where they lost to France.

He was also part of the side that finished third in Qatar, four years later.

After playing his part in McLaren's "wally with the brolly" moment at Wembley in the 2008 Euro qualifiers, Modric helped Croatia reach the quarter-finals in Austria and Switzerland.

Croatia's next internationals are in the in the Nations League - away to Czech Republic on 26 September and Spain on 29 September.

They then host England in the competition on 3 October, with the return fixture at Wembley on 12 November.
